arXiv:2604.02793v2 [quant-ph] 25 Aug 2026
Parity \notin\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0} \iff \mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0} is Fourier-Concentrated
Lucas Gretta
††thanks: University of California at Berkeley.  Email: lucas_gretta@berkeley.edu.  Supported by NSF Award CCF-2231095.
Meghal Gupta
††thanks: University of California at Berkeley.  Email: meghal@berkeley.edu.  Supported by NSF GRFP.
Malvika Raj Joshi
††thanks: University of California at Berkeley.  Email: malvika@berkeley.edu.  Supported by NSF grant 2311733 and DOE grant DE-SC0024124.
Abstract
A major open problem in understanding shallow quantum circuits ({\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}) is whether they can compute PARITY. In this work, we show that this question is solely about the Fourier spectrum of \mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}: any \mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0} circuit with non-negligible high-level Fourier mass suffices to exactly compute PARITY in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. Thus, proving a quantum analog of the seminal LMN theorem for {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} [22] is necessary to bound the quantum circuit complexity of PARITY.
In the other direction, LMN does not fully capture the limitations of {\mathsf{AC}}^{0}. For example, despite MAJORITY having 99\% of its weight on low-degree Fourier coefficients, no {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuit can non-trivially correlate with it [26, 28].
In contrast, we provide a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit that achieves (1-o(1)) correlation with MAJORITY, establishing the first average-case decision separation between {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} and {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. This suggests a uniquely quantum phenomenon: unlike in the classical setting, Fourier concentration may largely characterize the power of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.
PARITY is also known to be equivalent in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} to inherently quantum tasks such as preparing GHZ states to high fidelity. We extend this equivalence to a broad class of state-synthesis tasks. We demonstrate that existing measures such as trace distance, fidelity, and mutual information are insufficient to capture these states and introduce a new measure, felinity. We prove that preparing any state with non-negligible felinity, or derived states such as {\mathsf{poly}}(n)-weight Dicke states, implies \texttt{PARITY}\in\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}.

A Skipped proofs
1 Introduction
Understanding the computational power of constant-depth quantum circuits ({\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}) remains a central open problem in quantum complexity theory.
Classical constant-depth circuits ({\mathsf{AC}}^{0}) cannot compute PARITY [3, 10, 17] and in fact, form a strict hierarchy. Adding \texttt{PARITY}_{n} gates to {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} does not enable other hard computations such as arbitrary modular arithmetic or \texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}, making {\mathsf{AC}}^{0}\subsetneq{\mathsf{AC}}^{0}[2]\subsetneq{\mathsf{ACC}}\subseteq{\mathsf{TC}}^{0} [26, 28]. In contrast, {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} exhibits an “all-or-nothing” behavior [29]. The class {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}, obtained by augmenting {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} with PARITY gates (or its Hadamard conjugate FANOUT), can simulate all of {\mathsf{TC}}^{0} [23, 19]. Thus, determining whether {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} can compute PARITY, or equivalently, whether {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}={\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}, is a crucial step.
A distinctive feature of PARITY is that all of its Fourier mass lies on the highest-degree coefficient. However, {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuits exhibit strong concentration on low-degree Fourier coefficients, a landmark result known eponymously by LMN [22]. Subsequent works have led to a tight characterization of this Fourier spectrum [16, 30]. This suggests a natural approach to resolving whether \texttt{PARITY}\in{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} by seeking an analogous characterization for {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. The Fourier spectrum of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuits, induced by measuring the output qubit, has been conjectured to exhibit low degree concentration [24, 4], suggesting a quantum analog of LMN (“QLMN”) may hold. Informally, this conjecture states that the {\mathsf{poly}}(n)-level Fourier coefficients have negligible (n^{-\omega(1)}) weight. A fully parameterized version of this conjecture, analogous to the true LMN is stated in Conjecture 1.
Clearly, if the QLMN conjecture were true, then \texttt{PARITY}\not\in{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. In this work, we show that the reverse implication also holds:
\texttt{PARITY}\not\in{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}\Longleftrightarrow\mathrm{QLMN}.
In other words, proving QLMN is necessary for proving \texttt{PARITY}\not\in{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.
Another interpretation of our result is that any single-output {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit with non-negligible high-level Fourier mass (Definition 3.1) suffices to compute PARITY in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. This equivalence has no classical analog because adding a gate to {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} that only approximates some arbitrary high-degree boolean function, does not necessarily produce {\mathsf{AC}}^{0}[2].
An immediate consequence of our result is that any {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit achieving non-negligible correlation with \texttt{PARITY}_{n} on a random input provides a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit for computing \texttt{PARITY}_{n} exactly. Similarly, it suffices to construct a circuit with 1-1/{\mathsf{poly}}(n) correlation with \texttt{MAJORITY}_{n} on average, or a circuit with 1/{\mathsf{poly}}(n) advantage for MAJORITY in the worst case to obtain exact \texttt{PARITY}_{n}. These results and others are summarized in Table 1 below. Prior work of [13] introduced the worst-case bounded error classes \mathsf{BQAC}^{0}, \mathsf{BQTC}^{0}, and [12] subsequently showed \mathsf{BQTC}^{0}=\mathsf{BQAC}^{0}_{f} and \textsf{QTC}^{0}={\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}. In regards to these classes, our results imply that if \texttt{MAJORITY}\in\mathsf{BQAC}^{0}, then {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}={\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}.
An average-case separation.
MAJORITY is often used to illustrate limitations of Fourier-concentration for obtaining average-case {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} lower bounds. Despite the Majority function having 1-o(1) of its weight on low-degree Fourier coefficients, {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuits cannot achieve better than \Theta\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\right)-correlation with MAJORITY [26, 28]. We, however, show that a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit can achieve (1-1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)) correlation with \texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}. This establishes the first average-case decision problem separation between {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} and {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. Furthermore, this sharp contrast with the classical setting suggests that, in the quantum world, Fourier concentration may be largely sufficient to characterize {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. Indeed, by combining this result with our aforementioned hardness result, we see that the feasible regimes of MAJORITY in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} are essentially determined by QLMN.
Consequences for hardness of state synthesis.
It is well-known that preparing the cat state (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{0^{n}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{1^{n}}) or a nekomata state (\outerproduct*{0^n}{0^n}+\outerproduct*{1^n}{1^n}) in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} is equivalent to
computing PARITY in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. This equivalence also holds for preparing high-fidelity (i.e. 1-\varepsilon) approximations to these states [23, 27, 12].
However, we show that there are much weaker approximations whose preparation implies \texttt{PARITY}\in{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, but these cannot be distinguished from states known to be in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} through existing measures. To more extensively capture state synthesis tasks that are as hard as PARITY, we introduce a new notion, felinity (Definition 2.1). The felinity of a n-qubit state \rho directly quantifies the ability of a circuit for \rho to correlate with \texttt{PARITY}_{n}. Combined with our main result, this yields a large class of states whose preparation as black-box immediately unlock the full power of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}.
Another family of quantum states of interest is Dicke states, defined as uniform superpositions over n-bit strings of Hamming weight k (WLOG k\leq n/2).
Recent work shows that \texttt{FANOUT}_{n} enables preparation of arbitrary-weight states in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f} [21]. However, it was previously unknown whether this reliance on fanout is necessary. Using felinity, we show that \texttt{FANOUT}_{k} is necessary to prepare Dicke states of weight k.
Consequently, for any k={\mathsf{poly}}(n), such as k=n^{0.0001}, the ability to prepare weight-k Dicke states in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} would imply {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}={\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}.

1.1 Our results
We show that the Fourier concentration of {\mathsf{QAC}} functions is intimately related to the hardness of PARITY in {\mathsf{QAC}}. More formally, define {\mathsf{QAC}}(d,s) to be {\mathsf{QAC}} circuits with depth \leq d and size \leq s11
1
There is some subtlety based on whether {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} is defined to have polynomial ancillae or polynomial gates. In this paper this concern is largely not important, as our reductions achieve proportional blowup in both measures. and define the \text{QLMN}(\gamma(d,k)) to be the following proposition, parameterized based on a decay function \gamma:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}, similar to the way the classical [22] is parameterized.
Conjecture 1 (\text{QLMN}(\gamma) (folklore, [24, 4])).
For any d,s,n and all n-input C\in{\mathsf{QAC}}(d,s) with a designated output register t and let f_{C}(x):\{0,1\}^{n}\to[-1,1] denote the expected outcome of measuring Z_{t} on t. Then, for all k\in[n].
\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}\left[f_{\mathcal{C}}\right]<s\cdot\gamma(d,k)^{-1}.
Note that setting \gamma(d,k):=2^{\Omega\left(k^{1/d}\right)} would conjecture the analog of classical LMN. We show that proving strong lower bounds on the size/depth complexity of PARITY in {\mathsf{QAC}} necessitates proving QLMN under corresponding parameters.
Theorem 1.1 (Equivalence of QLMN and Hardness of Parity).
For all \gamma:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N},
\mathrm{QLMN}(\gamma)\iff\texttt{PARITY}_{n}\not\in{\mathsf{QAC}}(\Theta(d),\widetilde{\Theta}(\gamma(d,n))).
Equivalently, letting S(d,n) denote the maximum size such that no depth d circuit of this size can compute \texttt{PARITY}_{n}, then \text{QLMN}(\tilde{\Theta}\left(S(\Theta(d),k))\right) holds.
Here \Theta hides absolute constants, and \tilde{\Theta} hides absolute constants and log factors. Note that the dependence on circuit size on the LHS is baked into the QLMN definition. Restricting to the case of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, we have the following corollary.
Corollary 1.2.
\text{QLMN}({\mathsf{poly}}_{d}(k^{\omega(1)})) holds for some {\mathsf{poly}}_{d}(k^{\omega(1)}) if and only if \texttt{PARITY}\notin{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.
Next, we provide that a variety of approximation problems and state construction tasks that are {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete, or equivalently \textsf{QTC}^{0}-complete, under {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} reductions. Augmenting {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} gates with a “noisy” gate (and its inverse) for any one of the following tasks, provides the ability to implement any problem in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f} without error.
Theorem 1.3 ({\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete problems).
The following tasks are equivalent to exact FANOUTn under {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} reductions.
1.
Any non-negligible PARITYn correlation (Section 2.1.1). Achieving non-negligible (i.e. \geq 1/{\mathsf{poly}}(n)) correlation with \texttt{PARITY}_{n} on a random input.
2.
Weak nekomata-like states (Section 2.2). For any non-negl \varepsilon\geq 0, synthesizing a state \rho satisfying \braket{0^{n}|\rho|0^{n}}\geq\varepsilon,\braket{1^{n}|\rho|1^{n}}\geq\varepsilon.
3.
Poly-weight Dicke states (Section 2.2.1). For any \delta\in(0,1) and k=\Omega(n^{\delta})\leq n/2, synthesizing a state with at least (1-\varepsilon) fidelity with \ket{D^{n}_{k}}.
4.
High average case MAJORITYn correlation (Section 2.3). For any arbitrarily small constant \delta>0, achieving at least (1-1/n^{\delta}) correlation with \texttt{MAJORITY}_{n} on a random input.
5.
Bounded worst case MAJORITYn error (Section 2.3). For any \varepsilon=1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n),
achieving \varepsilon-correlation with \texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}({\bm{x}}) (correct wp \geq 1/2+\varepsilon/2) on every input {\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}.
In other words, a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C, whose m={\mathsf{poly}}(n) ancillae start in \ket{0^{m}}, for any one of the above tasks implies \mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}=\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}_{f}.
Notice that “weak-nekomata-like states” can have much lower fidelity and trace-distance to any nekomata compared to states trivially in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, such as \ket{0^{n}}. Moreover for small enough \varepsilon_{0},\varepsilon_{1}, they have much lower mutual information between qubits than the \ket{W_{n}} state (weight 1 Dicke state), which can be synthesized exactly in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} [12, 21].
To reliably discern these hard states, we introduce a new measure, felinity (Section 4.2), and show that preparing any state with non-negligible felinity implies {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}={\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f} (Section 2.2).
Finally, we crucially distinguish between average and worst case regimes for MAJORITY.
This is in contrast to \texttt{PARITY}_{n}, where average case and worst case error regimes for PARITY are equivalent for {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} as well as {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} (with randomness).
Both {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} and {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} can achieve \Theta(1/\sqrt{n})-correlation with MAJORITY, i.e., 1/2+\Theta(1/\sqrt{n}) success probability, on a random input by outputting the first input bit. It is also known that {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} cannot achieve better correlation than this for MAJORITY. However, our next result shows that this is not true for {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, thus establishing an average-case separation between the two classes.
Theorem 1.4 (Section 2.3.1 informal).
There exists a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit that achieves any (1-1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)) correlation with MAJORITY.
This brings us back to Moore’s original question of whether PARITY{}_{n}\in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. This question is indeed the key to determining the computational power of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, regardless of which notion of computation, exact/clean/approximate/average case/worst case, is used. Our results clear the path towards understanding {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} and motivate further study into the Fourier spectrum of \mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}. From a practical standpoint, it is sufficient to produce a gate for one of the much weaker approximation tasks from Theorem 1.3 to unlock the full power of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}, which includes modular arithmetic, QFT, sorting, and arbitrary Dicke state preparation [23, 11, 19, 29, 21].
1.2 Prior work
A key distinction between {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} and {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuits, arising from reversibility, is the role of FANOUT. In {\mathsf{AC}}^{0}, copying the outputs of gates is free. Quantumly, due to the no-cloning theorem, copying the output of gates is impossible. Instead, FANOUT refers to copying the classical information of a qubit. The reversible \texttt{FANOUT}_{n} gate copies a qubit onto n targets via XOR, and under Hadamard conjugation corresponds to a clean \texttt{PARITY}_{n} gate.
Foundational work by [23] established equivalences between \texttt{FANOUT}_{n}, \texttt{PARITY}_{n}, and cat/GHZ states (\ket{\hbox{\hbox to8.18pt{\vbox to8.43pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 4.08804pt\lower-3.20981pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.40042pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}{{}}{}{{{}}

\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}_{n}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{0^{n}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{1^{n}}). These can be thought of as complete problems under {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} reductions for the class obtained by including fan-out, {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}. Early works also showed that {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f} can implement arbitrary threshold functions, modular arithmetic, and more [23, 11, 19]. Subsequently, [27] discovered that preparing a “nekomata”, a weaker form of \ket{{}_{n}} consisting of a mixture rather than a superposition, is also {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete. They leveraged this new reduction to provide the first constant depth approximation of \texttt{PARITY}_{n} using exponential size. This allowed for approximate-\texttt{FANOUT}_{{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)} in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, which is limited to {\mathsf{poly}}(n) size. Thereafter,
[13] showed that threshold gates also provide the ability to create approximate nekomata. Recently both constructions were made exact by [12], implying that \textsf{QTC}^{0}={\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f} and \texttt{FANOUT}_{{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)} can be exactly implemented in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. Existing prior work on upper bounds and reductions is summarized in Table 1.
Prior work such as [13, 27] has focused mainly on worst-case error regimes, where performance is measured by the error guarantee for all inputs. [27] showed reductions between the worst-case approximations of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete problems. For high accuracy, such as (1-o(1)) fidelity with a nekomata or o(1) worst-case error for parity, [12]’s result implies {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-completeness by reducing from exact nekomata.
We also consider average-case regimes in Table 1, which are more natural from a Fourier-analytic standpoint. Average-case performance is measured by correlation with the target function on a uniformly random input. For \texttt{PARITY}_{n}, average-case error can be converted to worst-case error by mapping the input to a random string of the same parity, a transformation implementable in both {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} [32] and {\mathsf{AC}}^{0}22
2
provided access to random bits..
Analogous to the amplification possible in {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} via MAJORITY of parallel repetition, [20] showed that 1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)-correlation with \texttt{PARITY}_{n} can be amplified to exact \texttt{PARITY}_{n}.
Regarding upper bounds, known capabilities of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} have been limited. Existing constructions include regimes of parity, thresholds and symmetric functions matching {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} [27, 13]. In addition, [21] show that {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} can prepare constant-weight n-qubit Dicke states. It is unknown whether {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} contains all decision problems in {\mathsf{AC}}^{0}. The counterpart of this question, whether {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} contains problems outside {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} has been addressed to some degree.
Earlier works, [8, 32] established relational separations between the two classes. Recently, [12] was the first to establish a worst-case decision problem separating {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} and {\mathsf{AC}}^{0}.
They showed that \mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}\circ{\mathsf{NC}}^{0} contains {\mathsf{TC}}^{0}, a strictly more powerful class than {\mathsf{AC}}^{0}, demonstrating that even limited classical fanout (via multiple copies) significantly increases the power of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. The one-sided error in [12]’s construction is not achievable by {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} and forms the basis for their separation.
2 Technical Overview
We provide an overview of all our proof techniques organized as follows. In Section 2.1, we describe the equivalence to QLMN and the corollary leading to point (1) of Theorem 1.3. Next, in Section 2.2 we discuss the hardness of state preparations tasks which cover points (2,3) of Theorem 1.3. Finally, in Section 2.3 we focus on MAJORITY and discuss points (4,5) as well as the upper bound in Theorem 1.4. The full proofs are split into two sections, reductions (Section 4) and upper bounds (Section 5).
2.1 Characterizing {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f} Completeness
It is possible in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} to obtain a negligible but non-zero correlation with \texttt{PARITY}_{n} by hard-coding the answer to a small subset of the possible inputs. It is also possible to construct a state that has non-zero but negligible amplitude on the lower-weighted nekomata branch [27]. We show that any meaningful improvement over these approximations is as hard as exact parity.
Challenges and comparison to prior work.
Existing approaches for reducing from exact PARITY to approximate parity/nekomata regimes require sufficiently strong approximations. The “classical” approach involves first mapping the input to a uniformly random string of the same parity and amplifying by taking the MAJORITY of parallel runs. Since \texttt{MAJORITY}_{{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)} can be computed in {\mathsf{poly}}(n) size, this applies when the correlation with \texttt{PARITY}_{n} is at least 1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n) [20]. In contrast, the techniques we use to prove points (1,2,3) of Theorem 1.3 do not have classical analogues. This is because, arbitrary 1/{\mathsf{poly}}(n) correlations with \texttt{PARITY}_{n} cannot be black-box amplified in {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} since they require \texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}.
Prior inherently quantum approaches work by amplifying the weight on nekomata branches, but still require sufficient weight on both branches, \braket{0^{n}|\rho|0^{n}} and \braket{1^{n}|\rho|1^{n}}. Rosenthal’s nekomata amplification [27] applies to states with most of their weight on one nekomata branch and small but non-negligible weight on the other. The amplitude amplification techniques of [12], require a total constant weight on the two branches to amplify to the “good subspace” (supported only on \ket{0^{n}},\ket{1^{n}}) in constant depth.
Consequently, these methods do not apply to the regimes we consider, where the only guarantee is non-negligible weight on two branches. This forces us to dig deeper to pinpoint the additional structure in these approximation tasks.
2.1.1 Fourier concentration to Parity
Any n-input quantum circuit C with a designated output register has an associated real-valued Boolean function, f_{C}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to[-1,1]. This function is obtained by standard basis measurement distribution of the output qubit, or equivalently by the expected outcome on a Z observable.
For such functions f and 0\leq k\leq n, the weight above level k, \mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[f] is defined as [25],
\displaystyle\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[f]:=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq[n]\\
|S|\geq k\end{subarray}}\widehat{f}(S)^{2}.
(1)
This defines the Fourier mass of a n-input {\mathsf{QAC}} circuit C naturally through \widehat{f_{C}}.
Recall the definition of the QLMN proposition.
See 1
Note that \texttt{PARITY}_{n} does not have this type of concentration for any reasonable \gamma, since all the mass is on the degree n coefficient. Thus, the non-trivial direction is to show that a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C for which f_{C} is non-concentrated produces a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit for exact \texttt{PARITY}_{n}. Formally, we show the following.
See 1.1
This immediately provides the following consequences for approximate parity, thus proving point (1) of Theorem 1.3.
{restatable*}
[Non-negligible correlation with parity implies fanout]corollaryapproxtoexactpar
Let C be a depth d {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C using m ancillas whose designated output register achieves at least \varepsilon correlation with \texttt{PARITY}_{n}. Then, there exists a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C^{\prime} of depth d^{\prime}=O(d) using m^{\prime}=\tilde{O}((m+n)/\varepsilon) qubits that implements \texttt{FANOUT}_{n}.
The key step for this proof is a gadget which leverages C to construct a “nekomata-like” state that has constant amplitude on the \ket{0^{n}} branch and non-negligible amplitude on the subspace of strings with hamming weight at least k. From there, the following lemma suffices:
{restatable*}
[Threshold-block nekomata is {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete]lemmatwobranchdicke
Let C be a depth d, m ancilla circuit that constructs \ket{\psi}_{Q,A} with |Q|=n, satisfying,
\left\lVert\bra{0^{n}}_{Q}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq 1/2\quad\text{and}\quad\left\lVert{\Pi^{n}_{\geq k}}_{Q}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq\varepsilon
where \Pi^{n}_{\geq k} is the projector onto n-bit strings of Hamming weight at least k, for 0<k\leq n.
Then, there exists a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit of depth d^{\prime}=O(d) and m^{\prime}=O((m+n)/\varepsilon) that exactly implements \texttt{FANOUT}_{\ell} for \ell=k/\log^{2}k.
To prove this lemma, the idea is to partition the qubits into \ell blocks, and then apply an \mathtt{OR} gate onto a fresh ancilla. This partitioning is chosen at random. Next, we use amplitude amplification to remove the “bad” part which consists of the subspace orthogonal to \outerproduct*{0^n}{0^n}+\outerproduct*{1^n}{1^n}. This produces a state that has most of its weight on one nekomata branch and a small but non-negligible weight on the other and can be amplified to an exact nekomata through a combination of parallel and amplitude amplification. Through [27] this provides a circuit for fanout/parity. Furthermore, when k=n^{\delta}, this also provides a circuit for \texttt{FANOUT}_{n} with 1/\delta factor increase in depth.
We now state our key step.
{restatable*}[Fourier mass to Hamming slice]lemmathreshbranchwt
For any depth d, m-ancilla {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C acting on n inputs, there exists a depth O(d), m^{\prime}=m+2n+1-ancilla {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C^{*} that constructs a state \ket{\psi^{*}} satisfying
\left\lVert\bra{0^{n}}\cdot\ket{\psi^{*}}\right\rVert^{2}\geq 1/2\quad\text{and}\quad\left\lVert\Pi^{n}_{\geq k}\cdot\ket{\psi^{*}}\right\rVert^{2}\geq\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]/2.
for any 0<k\leq n. Here \Pi^{n}_{\geq k} is the projector onto n-bit strings of Hamming weight at least k.
First, given C, we obtain an “approximate clean computation” circuit C^{\prime} by using the standard copy-uncompute technique. This is done by first making a classical copy to preserve the input registers, then running C and applying a \mathtt{CNOT} gate on the output register and a fresh ancilla, and finally, “uncomputing” by applying all the previous gates in reverse (C^{\dagger} and the initial copy layer). When the output of C is boolean valued, f_{C}({\bm{x}})\in\{\pm 1\}, this transformation produces a clean computation of f_{C}, i.e,
\displaystyle\ket{{\bm{x}}}_{T}\ket{0^{m^{\prime}}}\mapsto_{C^{\prime}}\ket{{\bm{x}}}_{T}\ket{f_{C}({\bm{x}})}\ket{0^{m^{\prime}-1}}
(2)
(where we interpret \ket{f_{C}({\bm{x}})} as \in\left\{\ket{0},\ket{1}\right\} based on its Z eigenvalue).
Although Eq. 2 does not hold when the output qubit is non-deterministic, with f_{C}({\bm{x}})\in[-1,1], we can still bound the probability of the ancillae being returned to \ket{0^{m-1}} on a given input. We use this observation to prove the lemma for the state \ket{\psi^{*}}:=H^{\otimes n}_{T}C^{\prime}\ket{+^{n}}_{T}\ket{0^{m^{\prime}}} by post-selecting on the subspace containing \ket{0^{m-1}} on the non-output ancillae.
We show that the claimed overlap with \ket{0^{n}}_{T} follows simply by virtue of C being a single-output circuit, where, the variance of the measured output is bounded by 1/2. To argue about the amplitude in the subspace corresponding to \Pi^{n}_{\geq k}, we construct a special +1 eigenvector of \Pi^{n}_{\geq k}, \ket{\mathcal{T}_{k}}, based on the Fourier coefficients of f_{C}. This \ket{\mathcal{T}_{k}(C)} is essentially a gadget we design to extract the Fourier mass of f_{C} through the bilinear form,
\displaystyle\left(\bra{\mathcal{T}_{k}}\otimes\bra{-}\otimes\bra{0^{m^{\prime}-1}}\right)\ket{\psi^{*}_{C}}=\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]/2.
(3)
Since the overlap of \ket{\psi^{*}} with any +1 eigenvector of \left(\Pi^{n}_{\geq k}\otimes I\right) lower bounds the quantity \left\lVert\Pi^{n}_{\geq k}\cdot\ket{\psi^{*}}\right\rVert, this provides us the claimed bound.
2.2 Felinity as a measure of state preparation complexity
Existing notions of state approximation are insufficient to characterize states that are as hard as cat states in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. Taking fidelity for example, \braket{{}_{n}|0^{n}}^{2}=1/2, so it is not the case that all states of constant fidelity with \ket{{}_{n}} are hard. Fidelity with cat states/nekomata is only meaningful in this context when it is bounded above 1/2.
Another natural notion is based on mutual information between pairs of qubits.
A nekomata can be thought of as a mixture over n perfectly correlated classical bits. Thus, both nekomatas and Cat states have mutual information 1 between every pair of the n targets. On the other hand, there are states easily preparable in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, such as \ket{W_{n}}, with pairwise mutual information 1/n. For a mutual-information based state hardness metric, this suggests a high cutoff, eg \Omega(1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)). We show that states with much smaller pairwise mutual information, such as \varepsilon\ket{0^{n}}+\varepsilon\ket{1^{n}}+\ket{\perp}, and much lower fidelity with any nekomata are just as hard to construct as a nekomata in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.
The same issues arise when using other related metrics such as trace distance, phase-dependent-fidelity [27], or interaction information. We propose a new metric to quantify the complexity of state preparation tasks, felinity, parameterized by the number of targets n.
Definition 2.1 (Felinity of a quantum state).
For a n-qubit state \rho, the felinity of \rho, \mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho)\in[0,1] is defined as
\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho):=2\sum_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\braket{\bm{y}|\rho|\bm{y}}\cdot\braket{\bm{y}|X^{\otimes n}\rho X^{\otimes n}|\bm{y}}
Felinity has several natural properties, such as monotonicity, for any qubit q of \rho,
\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho)\leq\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n-1}}(\tr_{q}\rho),
(4)
and Lipschitz continuity (Lemma 4.3),
\displaystyle|\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho)-\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\sigma)|\leq 8\,\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma).
(5)
Felinity behaves as expected on the states discussed so far,
•
Any perfect n-nekomata \rho has \mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho)=1, the highest possible, and any \rho^{\prime} that is \varepsilon-close in trace distance to some nekomata has \mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho^{\prime})\geq 1-\Theta(\varepsilon).
•
For any n-qubit product state, \rho=\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2}\dots\rho_{n}, \mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho)\leq 2^{-n+1}=\mathrm{negl}(n).
•
Any n-qubit state \rho constructed by a {\mathsf{QNC}} circuit has \mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho)=\mathrm{negl}(n) (light-cone argument).
•
\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(W_{n})=0, and in a different basis, any \ket{\psi}=U^{\otimes n}\ket{W_{n}} has \mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\psi)\leq\mathrm{negl}(n) (See Lemma A.1)
•
Any state with non-negligible mass on a string \ket{\bm{y}} and the complement string \ket{\overline{\bm{y}}}, such as point (2) of Theorem 1.3, has non-negligible felinity.
We demonstrate that felinity captures {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-completeness of state preparation tasks by showing that a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit for constructing a n-qubit state with non-negligible felinity implies \texttt{PARITY}_{n}\in{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. The key step is the following lemma,
{restatable*}[Felinity gives advantage for parity]lemmaparfromfeln
Let \ket{\psi}=C\ket{0^{m}} be a state on m={\mathsf{poly}}(n) qubits constructed by a depth d {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C. Suppose that there exists a subset T of |T|=n qubits for which the state \rho_{T}=\tr_{\overline{T}}\outerproduct*{\psi}{\psi} has \mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho_{T})\geq\varepsilon. Then, there is a depth d^{\prime}=2d+4 circuit C^{\prime} on m^{\prime}=m+2 ancillas whose output achieves \geq|\varepsilon| correlation with \texttt{PARITY}_{n}.
We first recall the idea behind the Moore’s original reduction to Cat state [23, 27]. For any nekomata \ket{\nu_{n}}_{T,A} with n targets T and ancillae A, we have the following property. Let L be a layer of n \mathtt{CZ} gates each acting on an input qubit and a corresponding target from T. On any input {\bm{x}}, the state L\ket{\nu_{n}}_{T,A}\ket{{\bm{x}}} is orthogonal to \ket{\nu_{n}}_{T,A} iff {\bm{x}} has odd parity. To extract this information, we apply the reflection R=(I-2\outerproduct*{\nu_n}{\nu_n}_{T,A}\otimes\outerproduct*{+}{+}_{q}) on a fresh output register q, which acts as a controlled-X_{q} operator, controlled on T,A being \ket{\nu_{n}}. R can be implemented using the circuit C for \ket{\nu_{n}}, though,
\displaystyle R=C^{\dagger}\cdot(I-2\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m}\otimes\outerproduct*{+}{+}_{q})\cdot C
(6)
This provides a single-output circuit C^{\prime}=R\cdot L with an output register q for exactly computing \texttt{PARITY}_{n}. Back to the general case of Section 2.2, where C constructs an arbitrary state \ket{\psi}, we start by defining C^{\prime} the same way as above. Then, the focus of our proof is to relate the Fourier coefficients of f_{C^{\prime}} to \ket{\psi}.
Previous works generally treat the output of the circuit as a qubit or through the probability of measuring \ket{1} on the output register. We adopt a different but equivalent observables based viewpoint.
Specifically, f_{C^{\prime}}({\bm{x}}) as we defined in Definition 3.1 captures the expected \pm 1 outcome of measuring the Z observable on the output register q. Additionally, any Hermitian matrix \mathcal{O} is a valid observable corresponding to a measurement with possible outcomes among the eigenvalues of \mathcal{O}. Thus, we can associate the following 2^{n}\times 2^{n} observable with C^{\prime} by contracting the ancillae,
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{C^{\prime}}:=\bra{0^{m}}_{A}\otimes I\cdot\left(C^{\dagger}\cdot Z_{t}\otimes I\cdot C\right)\cdot\ket{0^{m}}_{A}\otimes I
(7)
This is essentially the Heisenberg evolution of the output measurement with eigenvalues in [-1,1]. Therefore, \braket{{\bm{x}}|\mathcal{O}_{C^{\prime}}|{\bm{x}}}=f_{C^{\prime}}({\bm{x}}). This re-interpretation of f_{C^{\prime}} allows us to cleanly expand its Fourier coefficients in terms of the quantities involved in Definition 2.1 for \rho_{T}, revealing that,
\displaystyle\widehat{f_{C^{\prime}}}([n])=\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho_{T}).
(8)
and hence \mathrm{corr}(f_{C^{\prime}},\texttt{PARITY}_{n})\geq\varepsilon. Then, Section 2.1.1 completes the reduction from exact \texttt{PARITY}_{n}, providing the following corollary.
{restatable*}[Non-negl felinity states are {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete]corollaryfelntofanout
Let \rho be any n-qubit state such that \mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho)=\varepsilon. If \rho can be constructed by a depth d, m={\mathsf{poly}}(n) ancilla circuit C, then there is a depth d^{\prime}=O(d), m^{\prime}=\tilde{O}((m+n)/\varepsilon) ancilla circuit to implement \texttt{FANOUT}_{n}.
As a consequence, preparing any non-negligible felinity state on n qubits in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, such as states in point (2) of Theorem 1.3, implies \mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}={\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}.
2.2.1 Dicke states imply parity
To demonstrate an application of felinity, we show that high-weight Dicke states can be turned into high-felinity states through a single layer of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} gates. When discussing Dicke states, \ket{D^{n}_{k}}, we without loss of generality consider the case when the weight k\leq n/2. This is because any \ket{D^{n}_{n-k}} can be obtained by negating the bits of \ket{D^{n}_{k}}.
This allows us to quantify the hardness of Dicke states as a function of k, and the {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}-complete states as those with k=n^{\delta} for any constant \delta\in(0,1). Then, we state the full version of point (3) of Theorem 1.3 below.
{restatable*}
[Dicke states imply Fanout]theoremdicketocat
Suppose there exists a depth d {\mathsf{QAC}} circuit C using m ancillas that, for some k\leq n/2, constructs a n-qubit state \rho satisfying,
\mathrm{TD}\left(\rho,\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right)\leq\frac{1}{80k},
Then, there is a depth d^{\prime}=O(d), m^{\prime}=m\cdot{\mathsf{poly}}(n)-ancilla {\mathsf{QAC}} circuit C^{\prime} that implements \texttt{FANOUT}_{k}.
Additionally, for \delta=\log k/\log n, there is a depth-O(d^{\prime}/\delta), O(m^{\prime}n^{1-\delta}) ancillae {\mathsf{QAC}} circuit for \texttt{FANOUT}_{n}.
To prove Section 2.2.1, the reduction of Section 2.1.1, which only uses classical gates does not suffice. Our key observation here is that \ket{D^{n}_{k}} has non-negligible overlap with the states \ket{p}^{\otimes n} and (Z\ket{p})^{\otimes n}, for p=k/n. Although \ket{p} and Z\ket{p} are far from orthogonal, for t\gg n/k, \ket{p}^{\otimes t} and (Z\ket{p})^{\otimes t}, have negligible overlap. Then, we show that \ket{D^{n}_{k}} can be transformed into a state \rho with non-negligible \mathcal{F}_{{}_{\ell}}(\rho), by applying a layer of \ell\approx k/\log k reflection gates, each acting as a controlled-not onto a fresh ancilla, with controls on \ket{\rho}^{\otimes t}. This reduces us to Section 2.2. Then, when k={\mathsf{poly}}(n), \delta is a constant, implying the following.
{restatable*}
[Preparing poly-weight Dicke state is {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete]corollarypolydickeisfanout
For any k=n^{\Theta(1)}, k\leq n/2, if there is a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit that prepares a n-qubit state \rho within 1/k trace distance of either \ket{D^{n}_{k}} or \ket{D^{n}_{n-k}}, then {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}={\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}.
Contrary to the equivalence between cat states and nekomatas, this reduction does not apply to an entangled version of a Dicke state, i.e a uniform mixture over strings of hamming weight k, rather than a superposition. Perhaps a more appropriate analogue of such a state is the “Poor-man’s cat state” which is a mixture over strings of odd parity and can be prepared in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, and in fact in {\mathsf{QNC}}^{0} [32]. As expected, the poor man’s cat state has \mathrm{negl}(n) felinity. The state \ket{{}_{n}} on the other hand, is a superposition over even parity strings (in the Hadamard basis), which is crucial to making its felinity 1.
In conclusion, felinity provides a concrete characterization of states that are hard to construct in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} and may be of interest to subsequent work on understanding the power of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} through the ancilla-only state synthesis setting.
2.3 Hardness classification of Majority regimes
MAJORITY is the canonical example used to illustrate the insufficiency of Fourier concentration lower bounds for {\mathsf{AC}}^{0}. In contrast, we show the feasible regimes of approximate MAJORITY in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} are fully determined by their Fourier concentration. First we obtain the following two corollaries as a consequence of Theorem 1.1, that show the remaining two points (4,5) of Theorem 1.3.
{restatable*}[High correlation with MAJORITY implies FANOUT]corollaryhardmajority
If there is a depth d, m-ancilla {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} whose output achieves at least (1-\frac{1}{n^{\delta}})-correlation with \texttt{MAJORITY}_{n} for any constant \delta>0, then, there exists a depth d^{\prime}=O(d), m^{\prime}={\mathsf{poly}}(m+n)-ancilla circuit that exactly implements \texttt{FANOUT}_{n}.
Then, the result follows directly from Corollary 4.2.
Next, since a worst case error of up to 1/{\mathsf{poly}}(n) for any function can be boosted to arbitrary (1-1/{\mathsf{poly}}(n))-correlation through parallel repetitions, we also have the following.
{restatable*}
[Worst-case approx MAJORITY implies FANOUT]corollaryhardworstmajority
Suppose there is a n-input \mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0} circuit C such that for all inputs {\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, measuring the output register of C results in \texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}({\bm{x}}) with probability at least 1/2+\varepsilon, for some \varepsilon\geq 1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n).
Then, \texttt{PARITY}_{n}\in\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}.
As a consequence, if \texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}\in\mathsf{BQAC}^{0}, i.e, can be computed with worst case error 1/3, then, \mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}=\mathrm{{\mathsf{QAC}}}^{0}_{f}.
Analogous {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} lower bounds to both these corollaries follow from [22]. However, much stronger {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} lower bounds for MAJORITY hold and are obtained from other techniques [26, 28]. We demonstrate next that these stronger bounds and techniques do not apply to {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.
2.3.1 Average case quantum advantage.
We show that {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuits can achieve (1-1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n))-correlation with MAJORITY on average. Classically, any randomized {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuit can be de-randomized while preserving its average case correlation [5]. However, randomness in quantum algorithms cannot be distilled in this manner and crucially, for inputs {\bm{x}} whose hamming weight is far from n/2, the output of our circuit is not deterministic.
[12] showed that the state \ket{W_{n}} can be constructed in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. We observe that any superposition of the states \ket{0^{n}} and \ket{W_{n}} can be constructed in {\mathsf{AC}}^{0}. Furthermore, we can implement the map \ket{0}\mapsto\ket{0^{n}} and \ket{1}\mapsto\ket{W_{n}} in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} (Lemma 5.2).
This allows us to implement the following map in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, which serves as a “weak fanout” gadget.
{restatable*}
[Poor man’s n-fanout in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}]corollarypoormansfanoutmap
There exists a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit acting on an input qubit
x, that cleanly achieves the following mapping,
\ket{0}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}\mapsto\ket{0}_{x}\ket{0^{n}},\quad\ket{1}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}\mapsto\ket{1}_{x}\ket{1/n}^{\otimes n}.
where \ket{\varepsilon}:=\sqrt{\varepsilon}\ket{1}+\sqrt{1-\varepsilon}\ket{0} for \varepsilon\in[0,1].
Implementing Poor man’s n^{1.1}-fanout in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}
would imply \texttt{PARITY}\in{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} because the state \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{0}\ket{0^{n^{1.1}}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{1}\ket{1/n}^{n^{1.1}} can be made to have high felinity on \approx n^{0.1} targets after a change of basis, similar to our Dicke states reduction. Poor man’s n-fanout is sufficient for our purposes to amplify correlations with threshold functions.
We note that [13] were the first to show the existence of a gadget with these properties in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} (refer to their Appendix C). They do so by mapping an input \ket{{\bm{x}}} to the state \ket{W_{\bm{x}}} defined as,
\displaystyle\ket{W_{{\bm{x}}}}:=\sum_{i\in[n]}(-1)^{x_{i}}\ket{0^{i-1}10^{n-i}}.
(9)
We remark that a similar construction is likely possible using their gadget.
A uniformly random input has its hamming weight reasonably concentrated about n/2. Thus, at a high level our strategy is to approximate MAJORITY well on these strings. On input {\bm{x}}, we can apply the Poor man’s n-fanout gadget to each qubit to obtain n independent weak copies of the input, each of the form \ket{x_{1}/n}\ket{x_{2}/n}\dots\ket{x_{n}/n}. We show that the following test can be performed in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} on a weak copy of this form.
{restatable*}[Weak copy test]lemmaoneweakcopytest
For any threshold t\in[n], there exists a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C such that, for every {\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n} with \big||{\bm{x}}|-t\big|=O(\sqrt{n}\,{\mathsf{polylog}}(n)), the state \rho({\bm{x}}) on the designated register “\mathrm{out}” of C\ket{x_{1}/n}\cdots\ket{x_{n}/n}\ket{0}_{\mathrm{out}} satisfies,
\braket{0|\rho({\bm{x}})|0}=1-\lambda_{t}(1+o(1))\left(\frac{|{\bm{x}}|-t}{n}\right)^{2}
where \lambda_{t}=\frac{e^{-t/n}}{1+t^{2}/n^{2}}=\Theta(1).
Then, amplifying using the n weak copies and a={\mathsf{polylog}}(n) fanout, we obtain a circuit that outputs 1 with probability at least 1-1/n if \big||{\bm{x}}|-t\big|<\frac{\sqrt{n}}{2a}, and outputs 0 with probability at least 1-1/n if \big||{\bm{x}}|-t\big|>\frac{\sqrt{n}}{a} (Lemma 5.6). Finally, we perform this test for {\mathsf{polylog}}(n) values of t spaced out to cover the interval concentrated about n/2\pm\sqrt{n}/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n). Choosing these values of t carefully gives the desired correlation with MAJORITY stated below.
{restatable*}[(1-1/{\mathsf{polylog}}(n))-correlation with Majority in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}]theoremezmajority
For any constant c, there exists a d:=d(c) such that there is a family of {\mathsf{QAC}} circuits of depth d and size {\mathsf{poly}}_{c}(n) that achieve (1-1/\log^{c}(n)) correlation with MAJORITY.
Combining with existing lower bounds of [26, 28] for {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} gives the following separation.
Corollary 2.2 (Average-case constant-depth quantum advantage).
There exist Boolean functions f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} that have o(1) correlation with any {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuit, yet have 1-o(1) correlation with some {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit.
3 Preliminaries
A depth-d \mathsf{QAC} circuit on n input qubits and m ancilla qubits initialized to \ket{0^{m}} consists of d layers of multi-qubit gates, in which each qubit participates in at most one gate, and arbitrary single-qubit unitaries taken to be free. We adopt the formulation of [27], where each multi-qubit gate is a reflection about a product state. Formally, a gate G(S) on subset S of qubits has the form G(S)=(I-2\outerproduct*{\vth}{\vth}_{S}) for some product state \ket{\vec{\theta}}_{S}. The single qubit unitaries are arbitrary and do not contribute to the depth. This is equivalent to [23]’s original definition where each multi-qubit gate is a Toffoli gate [27].
In most prior works on {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, the output of a circuit on input {\bm{x}} is given by the probability of measuring \ket{1} on a designed register t. We consider an equivalent observables-based definition, which is more natural in the context of boolean analysis.
Definition 3.1 (Single output circuit).
Let C be a n-input {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit acting on m ancillae, with a designated target register t. The output of C on input {\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n} is a randomized variable \in\{\pm 1\}, given by the outcome of measuring the observable Z_{t}\otimes I on C\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{0^{m}}. The associated real-valued boolean function computed by C, f_{C}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{\pm 1\}, describes the expected output on input {\bm{x}},
f_{C}({\bm{x}}):=\braket{{\bm{x}},0^{m}|C^{\dagger}\cdot Z_{t}\otimes I\cdot C|{\bm{x}},0^{m}}
We also consider {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} state preparation circuits that do not act on any input qubits—instead starting with \ket{0^{m}} on all registers. In this case, the parameter n refers to the number of qubits in the target state and m is required to be {\mathsf{poly}}(n).
Definition 3.2 (State preparation circuit).
A circuit C prepares an n-qubit state \ket{\psi}_{X} using m qubits if,
C\ket{0^{m}}=\ket{\psi}_{X}\ket{\varphi}
for some state \ket{\varphi}, unentangled with \ket{\psi}_{X} on the remaining qubits. Furthermore C cleanly prepares \ket{\psi}_{X} if \ket{\varphi}=\ket{0^{m-n}}.
All our state construction upper bounds are clean preparations. When proving reductions, we don’t enforce clean preparations.
3.1 Notation
We use contractions such as \bra{\nu}_{T} on states acting on larger sub-systems, \ket{\psi}_{T,A}. The notation \bra{\nu}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}_{T,A} refers to the un-normalized vector obtained by tracing out the T sub-system in \outerproduct*{\nu}{\nu}_{T}\otimes I_{A}\cdot\ket{\psi}. We also use the shorthand \bra{\psi}\cdot M\cdot\ket{\psi} for the operator given by (\bra{\psi}\otimes I)M(\ket{\psi}\otimes I) when it is clear that the matrix M acts on space larger than \ket{\psi}. Then, Definition 3.1 can be rewritten, f_{C}({\bm{x}}):=\braket{{\bm{x}},0^{m}|C^{\dagger}Z_{t}C|{\bm{x}},0^{m}}
For 0\leq\varepsilon\leq 1, we define \ket{\varepsilon} to be the single-qubit state given by \ket{\varepsilon}=\sqrt{\varepsilon}\ket{1}+\sqrt{1-\varepsilon}\ket{0}. This is consistent with the usual definitions of \ket{0},\ket{1}. For 0\leq\gamma\leq 1, define \mathrm{Rot}_{\gamma} to be the single-qubit unitary
\displaystyle\mathrm{Rot}_{\gamma}:=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{\gamma}&\sqrt{1-\gamma}\\
\sqrt{1-\gamma}&-\sqrt{\gamma}\end{bmatrix}.
(10)
3.1.1 {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-completeness
{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f} can be equivalently defined as the quantum analog of {\mathsf{TC}}^{0}, consisting of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} and arbitrary THRESHOLD{}^{n}_{k} gates, i.e, {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}=\textsf{QTC}^{0} [19, 13, 12]. The notion of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-completeness can be viewed as the quantum analog of {\mathsf{TC}}^{0}-completeness [1]. Augmenting {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} gates with a gate for any {\mathsf{TC}}^{0}-complete problem provides the ability to implement any other problem in {\mathsf{TC}}^{0}. Canonical {\mathsf{TC}}^{0}-complete problems (under {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} reductions) consist of sorting, integer division and iterated multiplication [9, 18], but notably do not include \texttt{PARITY}_{n} ({\mathsf{AC}}^{0}[2]\subsetneq {\mathsf{TC}}^{0}) [26, 28]. On the other hand, {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete problems (under {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} reductions) include PARITY, MAJORITY and state synthesis of any nekomata (uniform mixture of \ket{0^{n}} and \ket{1^{n}}) [23, 27, 13].
3.2 Analysis of boolean functions
In boolean analysis it is convenient to have f({\bm{x}})\in\{\pm 1\}.
To accommodate standard basis inputs of the form \ket{{\bm{x}}} where {\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, we define boolean functions such as PARITY, MAJORITY as \{0,1\}^{n}\to\{\pm 1\} instead of \{\pm 1\}^{n}\to\{\pm 1\}.
For a string {\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, we use \left\lvert{\bm{x}}\right\rvert to denote the hamming weight of {\bm{x}}. Then, \texttt{PARITY}_{n}({\bm{x}}):=(-1)^{|{\bm{x}}|} and we use the following convention for MAJORITY,
\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}({\bm{x}}):=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }|{\bm{x}}|\leq n/2,\\
-1&\text{if }|{\bm{x}}|>n/2.\end{cases}
A powerful technique for analyzing boolean functions is their Fourier decomposition, for a reference we point the reader to [25]. The characters \chi_{S}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} defined by \chi_{S}(x):=(-1)^{\oplus_{i\in S}x_{i}} form an orthonormal basis for the vector space of real-valued boolean functions. Projecting f onto this basis reveals the Fourier decomposition of f,
f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\hat{f}(S)\chi_{S}(x).
(11)
By Parseval’s, \sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\hat{f}(S)^{2}=1. The correlation of real valued boolean functions is defined by:
Definition 3.3 (Correlation of real valued boolean functions ).
The correlation of two boolean functions f,g:\{0,1\}^{n}\to[-1,1] is defined as,
\mathrm{corr}(f,g):=\Ex_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}f({\bm{x}})g({\bm{x}}).
By Parseval’s again, \mathrm{corr}(f,g)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\widehat{f}(S)\cdot\widehat{g}(S).
Recall the real-valued boolean function f_{C}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to[-1,1] associated with the output of C, from Definition 3.1.
Definition 3.4 ({\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit correlation with boolean function).
Given a circuit C on n input qubits and m ancilla A, with a designated output register t, the correlation of C with a boolean function g({\bm{x}}):\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{\pm 1\}, \mathrm{corr}(C,g) is defined to the correlation between f_{C} and g, given by,
\displaystyle\mathrm{corr}(f_{C},g)
\displaystyle:={\mathsf{E}}_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}f_{C}({\bm{x}})g({\bm{x}})
\displaystyle={\mathsf{E}}_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}\braket{{\bm{x}},0^{m}|C^{\dagger}Z_{t}C|{\bm{x}},0^{m}}g({\bm{x}})
3.3 Procedures in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}
Note the following form of the standard un-computing ancillae technique for quantum circuits due to [6]. We include a proof of this specific formulation in Appendix A.
Claim 3.5 (Approximate clean computation [6]).
Let C be a n-input depth d single-output {\mathsf{QAC}} circuit using m ancillae such that, on input {\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, the output register measures to \ket{0} with probability p_{0}({\bm{x}}) and 1 with probability p_{1}({\bm{x}})=1-p_{0}({\bm{x}}).
Then there exists a n-input {\mathsf{QAC}} circuit C^{\prime} of depth O(d) with m^{\prime}=m+n+1 ancillae such that for all {\bm{x}}, conditioning on the non-output registers being clean produces the (unnormalized) vector,
\bra{0^{m^{\prime}-1}}_{A}\cdot C^{\prime}({\bm{x}})\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{0^{m^{\prime}}}_{A,t}=p_{0}({\bm{x}})\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{0}_{t}+p_{1}({\bm{x}})\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{1}_{t}
In other words, C^{\prime}\cdot\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{0^{m^{\prime}}} has amplitude exactly p_{b}({\bm{x}}) on \ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{b}\ket{0^{m^{\prime}-1}}, and all the non-output registers are returned to their starting state with probability p_{0}({\bm{x}})^{2}+p_{1}({\bm{x}})^{2}.
We will also need the following primitives.
Fact 3.6.
Let {\mathsf{R}}_{\ket{\psi}}:=I-2\outerproduct{\psi}{\psi}.
If state \ket{\psi}\ket{0^{n}} can be constructed by a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}(d,s) circuit acting on \ket{0^{m}}, then {\mathsf{R}}_{\ket{\psi}} can be implemented by a depth 2d+1 {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}(2d+1,2s+1) circuit with the same number of ancillae.
Fact 3.7 (Poly-logarithmic Fanout in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} [27, 12]).
For any k={\mathsf{polylog}}(n),
\texttt{FANOUT}_{k}\in{\mathsf{QAC}}(\Theta(1),{\mathsf{poly}}(n)).
[13] also showed that the exact amplitude amplification technique of [15, 7] can be performed in {\mathsf{QAC}}. We will use the following sub-routines that are equivalent in the single-round special case.
Fact 3.8 (Claim 2.4 of [20]).
Suppose there exists a depth-d m-qubit {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit to construct \ket{\psi}_{T,A}=C\ket{0^{m}} satisfying,
\left\lVert\bra{0^{n}}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq 1/4,\quad\text{and}\quad\left\lVert\bra{1^{n}}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq 1/4.
Then, there is a circuit C^{\prime} of depth d^{\prime}\leq 3(d+2) using m^{\prime}=m+2 ancillae that exactly synthesizes an n-nekomata.
Claim 3.9.
Let \ket{\psi} be any n qubit state. Suppose there exists a depth-d m-ancilla {\mathsf{QAC}} circuit C that cleanly prepares the following n+1-qubit state \ket{\varphi},
\ket{\varphi}_{T,t}=\sqrt{\alpha}\ket{\psi}_{T}\ket{1}_{t}+\sqrt{1-\alpha}\ket{\mathrm{bad}}_{T}\ket{0}_{t},
for some \alpha\geq 1/5.
Then, there exists a depth-3d+2 {\mathsf{QAC}} circuit C^{\prime} that cleanly constructs \ket{\psi}, i.e, C^{\prime}\ket{0^{m+n+2}}=\ket{\psi}\ket{0^{m+2}}.
Proof.
Let \gamma:=1/(2\alpha), and let \mathsf{c}\text{-}{\mathsf{R}}_{\gamma} denote the controlled {\mathsf{R}}_{\gamma} gate.
Using a fresh ancilla a, we can prepare the following state cleanly in depth d+1,
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{0}}
\displaystyle:=\mathsf{c}\text{-}{\mathsf{R}}_{\gamma}(t,a)\cdot\ket{\varphi}_{T,t}\ket{0}_{a}
(12)
\displaystyle=\sqrt{\alpha}\ket{\psi}_{T}\ket{1}_{a}{\mathsf{R}}_{\gamma}\ket{0}_{t}+\sqrt{1-\alpha}\ket{\mathrm{bad}}_{T}\ket{0}_{a}\ket{0}_{t}
(13)
\displaystyle=1/2\ket{\psi}_{T}\ket{1}_{a}\ket{1}_{t}+\sqrt{3}/2\ket{\mathrm{bad}^{\prime}}_{T,t}\ket{0}_{a}
(14)
Applying a Z gate on a, we obtain,
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{1}}
\displaystyle:=-1/2\ket{\psi}_{T}\ket{1}_{a}\ket{1}_{t}+\sqrt{3}/2\ket{\mathrm{bad}^{\prime}}_{T,t}\ket{0}_{a}.
(15)
Then, applying {\mathsf{R}}_{\ket{\psi_{0}}} which can be implemented in depth 2d+1 by Fact 3.6, we obtain
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{2}}
\displaystyle:=(I-2\outerproduct*{\psi_0}{\psi_0})\ket{\psi_{1}}
(16)
\displaystyle=\ket{\psi}\ket{1}_{t,a}.
(17)
Finally to clean up, we can apply X gates to t,a without increasing depth.
∎
4 Fourier spectrum of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}
We will first show a key connection between the Fourier mass at levels \geq k of a circuit and synthesis of nekomata-like states.
\threshbranchwt
Proof.
Let C^{\prime} be the approximate clean computation circuit obtained from C through Claim 3.5, such that under the following register labeling, for any {\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n},
\displaystyle\bra{0^{m^{\prime}-1}}_{A}\cdot C^{\prime}\ket{{\bm{x}}}_{X}\ket{0^{m^{\prime}}}_{A,t}
\displaystyle=\ket{{\bm{x}}}_{X}\left(p_{0}({\bm{x}})\ket{0}+p_{1}({\bm{x}})\ket{1}\right)_{t}.
(18)
Note this vector is not necessarily a normalized state. Now consider the resulting state on input \ket{+^{n}},
\displaystyle\ket{\psi}:=C^{\prime}\ket{+^{n}}_{X}\ket{0^{a+1}}_{A,t}
(19)
We will show \ket{\psi^{*}}=H^{\otimes}_{X}\ket{\psi} has the required amplitudes on the X register.
Required amplitude on \ket{0^{n}} branch.
From Eq. 19,
\displaystyle\left\lVert\bra{+^{n}}_{X}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert
\displaystyle\geq\left\lVert\bra{+^{n+1}}_{X,t}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert
(20)
\displaystyle\geq\bra{+^{n+1}}_{X,t}\bra{0^{m^{\prime}-1}}_{A}\cdot\ket{\psi}
(21)
\displaystyle=\bra{+^{n+1}}_{X,t}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n}}}\sum_{{\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}p_{0}({\bm{x}})\ket{{\bm{x}}}_{X}\ket{0}_{t}+p_{1}({\bm{x}})\ket{{\bm{x}}}_{X}\ket{1}_{t}\right)
(22)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{{\bm{x}},\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\braket{\bm{y}|{\bm{x}}}\cdot\bra{+}_{t}\cdot\left(p_{0}({\bm{x}})\ket{0}+p_{1}({\bm{x}})\ket{1}\right)_{t}
(23)
\displaystyle=\Ex_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}\left[\frac{p_{0}({\bm{x}})+p_{1}({\bm{x}})}{\sqrt{2}}\right]\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\text{(use $\braket{{\bm{x}}|\bm{y}}=\delta_{{\bm{x}},\bm{y}}$)}
(24)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
(25)
Thus \left\lVert\bra{0^{n}}\cdot\ket{\psi^{*}}\right\rVert^{2}\geq\frac{1}{2}.
Required amplitude on threshold branch.
For any +1 eigenstate \ket{\mathcal{T}_{k}} of \Pi^{n}_{\geq k},
\displaystyle\left\lVert\Pi^{n}_{\geq k}\cdot\ket{\psi^{*}}\right\rVert\geq\left\lVert\bra{\mathcal{T}_{k}}\cdot\ket{\psi^{*}}\right\rVert.
(26)
We will construct a \ket{\mathcal{T}_{k}} that serves as a gadget to extract the Fourier mass. Re-label the standard basis vectors \ket{\bm{y}} for \bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n} to \ket{S} for S\subseteq[n], by mapping each string to its corresponding subset. Consider the following eigenstate,
\displaystyle\ket{\mathcal{T}_{k}}
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma_{k}}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq[n]\\
|S|\geq k\end{subarray}}\widehat{f_{C}}(S)\ket{S}
(27)
where, \gamma_{k}=\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[f_{C}], ensuring \ket{\mathcal{T}_{k}} is normalized. In the Hadamard basis,
\displaystyle\ket{\widehat{T_{k}}}
\displaystyle:=H^{\otimes n}\ket{\mathcal{T}_{k}}
(28)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma_{k}}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq[n]\\
|S|\geq k\end{subarray}}\widehat{f_{C}}(S)\ket{\vec{-}}_{S}\ket{\vec{+}}_{\overline{S}}.
(29)
Using Eq. 19,
\displaystyle\left\lVert\bra{\mathcal{T}_{k}}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert
\displaystyle\geq\left\lvert\bra{\widehat{T_{k}}}_{T}\bra{-}_{t}\bra{0^{m^{\prime}-1}}_{A}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rvert
(30)
\displaystyle\geq\bra{\widehat{T_{k}}}_{T}\bra{-}_{t}\bra{0^{m^{\prime}-1}}_{A}\cdot\ket{\psi}
(31)
\displaystyle=\bra{\widehat{T_{k}}}_{T}\bra{-}_{t}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n}}}\sum_{{\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\ket{{\bm{x}}}\left(p_{0}({\bm{x}})\ket{0}+p_{1}({\bm{x}})\ket{1}\right)\right)
(32)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n}}}\sum_{{\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\braket{\widehat{\mathcal{T}_{k}}|{\bm{x}}}\cdot\underbrace{\left(p_{0}({\bm{x}})-p_{1}({\bm{x}})\right)}_{f_{C}({\bm{x}})/\sqrt{2}}
(33)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 2^{n}\cdot\gamma_{k}}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}\\
S\subseteq[n],|S|\geq k\end{subarray}}\widehat{f_{C}}(S)\cdot\underbrace{\left(\bra{\vec{-}}_{S}\bra{\vec{+}}_{\overline{S}}\right)\cdot\ket{{\bm{x}}}}_{2^{-n/2}\cdot\chi_{S}({\bm{x}})}\cdot f_{C}({\bm{x}})
(34)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\gamma_{k}}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq[n]\\
|S|\geq k\end{subarray}}\widehat{f_{C}}(S)\cdot\Ex_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}\chi_{S}({\bm{x}})\cdot f_{C}({\bm{x}})
(35)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\gamma_{k}}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq[n]\\
|S|\geq k\end{subarray}}\widehat{f_{C}}(S)^{2}
(36)
\displaystyle=\sqrt{\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]/2}.
(37)
Therefore, from Eq. 26, \left\lVert\Pi^{n}_{\geq k}\cdot\ket{\psi^{*}}\right\rVert^{2}\geq\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]/2.
∎
To prove the equivalence between Conjecture 1 and \texttt{PARITY}_{n}, we will first reduce \texttt{PARITY}_{n} to the following weak-nekomata state which we show is {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete.
Lemma 4.1 (Skewed nekomata to exact parity).
Let C be a depth-d {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit acting on m qubits that constructs the state \ket{\psi}_{T,A}=C\ket{0^{m}} satisfying \left\lVert\outerproduct*{0^n}{0^n}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq 1/4 and \left\lVert\outerproduct*{1^n}{1^n}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq\varepsilon for some non-negligible \varepsilon.
Then, there exists a depth d^{\prime}=O(d) circuit that, using m^{\prime}=m\cdot{\mathsf{poly}}(n) ancillae prepares an exact nekomata state.
Proof.
WLOG, for a real and non-negative \gamma\geq 1/2 the state \ket{\psi} can be written as
\displaystyle\ket{\psi}
\displaystyle=\sqrt{\gamma}\ket{0^{n}}_{T}\ket{\alpha_{0}}_{A}+\sqrt{\varepsilon}\ket{1^{n}}_{T}\ket{\alpha_{1}}_{A}+\sqrt{1-\gamma-\varepsilon}\ket{\perp}_{T,A}.
(38)
Now, using a fresh ancilla a and two gates controlled on \ket{0^{n}} and \ket{1^{n}} to mark the nekomata branches, we obtain
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{1}}
\displaystyle=(I-2\outerproduct*{0^n}{0^n}\otimes\outerproduct*{+}{+}_{a})\cdot(I-2\outerproduct*{1^n}{1^n}\otimes\outerproduct*{+}{+}_{a})\cdot\ket{\psi}\ket{0}_{a}
(39)
\displaystyle=\sqrt{\gamma}\ket{0^{n}}_{T}\ket{\alpha_{0}}_{A}\ket{1}_{a}+\sqrt{\varepsilon}\ket{1^{n}}_{T}\ket{\alpha_{1}}_{A}\ket{1}_{a}+\sqrt{1-\gamma-\varepsilon}\ket{\perp}_{T,A}\ket{0}_{a}.
(40)
Then we apply Claim 3.9 to amplify the “good” amplitude and discard the cleaned up a register to produce the state
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{1}}
\displaystyle=\sqrt{1-\varepsilon_{1}}\ket{0^{n}}_{T}\ket{\alpha_{0}}_{A}+\sqrt{\varepsilon_{1}}\ket{1^{n}}_{T}\ket{\alpha_{1}}_{A}.
(41)
where \varepsilon_{1}=\varepsilon/\gamma\geq\varepsilon is still non-negligible.
Next observe that the parallel amplification technique of [27] can now be used to obtain a high fidelity nekomata using m_{1}:=\Theta(1/\varepsilon_{1}^{2}) copies and one layer.
Imagine arranging these copies into a grid, each copy in a row. Then for each column i\in[n], apply an OR of all qubits with output unto a fresh register q_{i}. The registers Q=\left\{q_{1}\dots q_{n}\right\} now make up the new nekomata targets. To see this, the probability of this measuring to all 0 is
\displaystyle\left\lVert\bra{0^{n}}_{Q}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}
\displaystyle=\left(\sqrt{1-\varepsilon_{1}}\right)^{2m_{1}}\approx 1/e.
(42)
The remaining probability is all 1s.
This produces a high-fidelity approximation of a nekomata, allowing us to apply Fact 3.8 to obtain an exact nekomata and thus \texttt{FANOUT}_{n} or \texttt{PARITY}_{n}.
∎
We now show that a generalized “threshold-block” nekomata is {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete.
\twobranchdicke
Proof.
Let D be the distribution over \{0,1\}^{n} supported on strings of Hamming weight at least k given by the squared amplitudes of \frac{\Pi^{n}_{\geq k}\ket{\psi}}{\left\lVert\Pi^{n}_{\geq k}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert} in standard basis.
Then we will show there exist \ell=\Theta\!\left(\frac{k}{\log^{2}k}\right) disjoint nonempty subsets S_{1},\dots,S_{\ell}\subseteq[n] such that
\displaystyle\Pr_{{\bm{x}}\sim D}\!\left[\forall j\in[\ell],\;{\bm{x}}|_{S_{j}}\not\equiv 0\right]\geq c
(43)
for some absolute constant c>0.
Let \ell=\left\lfloor\frac{k}{\log^{2}k}\right\rfloor. Partition [n] uniformly at random into \ell nonempty disjoint sets S_{1},\dots,S_{\ell} of (almost) equal size. Then for every j,
\displaystyle|S_{j}|\geq\frac{n}{2\ell}.
(44)
Note the standard bound for any t\geq k,
\frac{\binom{n-|S_{j}|}{t}}{\binom{n}{t}}\leq\left(1-\frac{|S_{j}|}{n}\right)^{t}\leq e^{-t|S_{j}|/n}\leq e^{-k/(2\ell)}=e^{-\Theta(\log^{2}k)}.
Fix any x\in\{0,1\}^{n} with Hamming weight t\geq k, and let T=\mathrm{supp}(x). For a fixed j,
\displaystyle\Pr[T\cap S_{j}=\varnothing]
\displaystyle=\frac{\binom{n-|S_{j}|}{t}}{\binom{n}{t}}\leq e^{-\Theta(\log^{2}k)}.
(45)
By a union bound over all \ell blocks,
\displaystyle\Pr[\exists j:T\cap S_{j}=\varnothing\big]\leq\ell\cdot e^{-\Theta(\log^{2}k)}.
(46)
Since \ell\leq k, the right-hand side is o(1), and in particular for large enough k,
\Pr[\forall j,\;T\cap S_{j}\neq\varnothing\big]\geq\frac{9}{10}.
(47)
Thus, for a random partition, every fixed x of weight at least k hits all \ell blocks with \Omega(1) probability. Averaging over x\sim D implies that there exists a fixed choice of S_{1},\dots,S_{\ell} achieving the desired bound.
Apply an \mathtt{OR} gate for each of these subsets onto a fresh ancilla. Then, Lemma 4.1 completes the reduction.
∎
Using this reduction, we can now prove the equivalence between PARITY and QLMN.
4.1 Parity equivalence of Quantum LMN
Corollary 4.2 (High Degree Fourier mass to PARITY computation).
Suppose there exists a depth d, m-ancilla single-output {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C acting on n inputs, such that for some k\geq n^{\delta},
\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]\geq\varepsilon,
then, there exists a depth O(d), O((m+n)\cdot\log^{2}(k)/\varepsilon)-ancilla {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C^{\prime} for \texttt{PARITY}_{k} and a depth O(d/\delta),\tilde{O}((m+n)\cdot n^{1-\delta}/\varepsilon)-ancilla {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit for \texttt{PARITY}_{n}.
Proof.
By Section 2.1.1 we can construct a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C^{\prime} that prepares a state \ket{\psi} satisfying
\left\lVert\bra{0^{n}}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq 1/2 and \left\lVert\Pi^{n}_{\geq k}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq\varepsilon/2.
Therefore, if \varepsilon is non-negligible, Section 2.1.1 implies a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit for for \texttt{PARITY}_{k/\log^{2}k} with O(d) depth, and O((m+n)/\varepsilon) ancilla. By the classical divide and conquer argument, there exists a O(d) depth, O((m+n)\log^{2}(n)/\varepsilon) ancilla {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit for \texttt{PARITY}_{k}, and a circuit for \texttt{PARITY}_{n} with a O(1/\delta) multiplicative blowup in depth and n^{1-\delta} blowup in ancillae.
∎
We now have all the pieces to complete the proof of Theorem 1.1.
See 1.1
Proof.
Let S(d,n) denote the maximum size such that no depth d {\mathsf{QAC}} circuit of this size can compute \texttt{PARITY}_{n}.
We first prove the RHS implies the LHS. Let C be any single-output, n-input {\mathsf{QAC}}(d,s) circuit.
By Corollary 4.2, there exists a {\mathsf{QAC}}\left(\Theta(d),\Theta\left(\frac{s\cdot\log^{2}(k)}{W^{\geq k}[f_{\mathcal{C}}]}\right)\right) circuit for computing \texttt{PARITY}_{k} (as the ancilla blowup is proportional to the size blowup). Therefore \frac{s}{W^{\geq k}[f_{\mathcal{C}}]}>\tilde{\Theta}(S(\Theta(d),k)) (as clearly S(d,k)\geq k), and hence s\cdot\tilde{\Theta}\left(S(\Theta(d),k)\right)^{-1}>W^{\geq k}[f_{\mathcal{C}}], which implies \text{QLMN}\left(\tilde{\Theta}\left(S(\Theta(d),k)\right)\right). Note that for any \gamma such that the RHS holds S\geq\gamma, and so does \text{QLMN}\left(\tilde{\Theta}\left(\gamma(\Theta(d),k)\right)\right).
The other direction is simpler. Suppose \text{QLMN}(\gamma) holds. Then any {\mathsf{QAC}}(d,s) circuit for computing \texttt{PARITY}_{k} must have s>\gamma(d,k) and so \texttt{PARITY}_{k}\not\in{\mathsf{QAC}}(d,\gamma(d,k)). Appropriate reparameterizations give the stated form.
∎
4.1.1 Consequences for {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete problems
We now present some consequences of the equivalence of QLMN and \texttt{PARITY}\not\in{\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} for {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete problems. The first of which is the uniquely quantum phenomenon that any non-negligible correlation with \texttt{PARITY}_{n} can be boosted to exact-\texttt{PARITY}_{n} in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.
\approxtoexactpar
Proof.
The correlation of f_{C} with \texttt{PARITY}_{n} is equivalent to \mathbf{W}^{n}[f_{C}]. Therefore the statement follows from Corollary 4.2.
∎
We also show that any circuit that achieves high correlation with MAJORITY suffices to compute FANOUT.
\hardmajority
Proof.
Assume WLOG that n is odd, otherwise obtain a similar correlation for \texttt{MAJORITY}_{n-1} by using an extra ancilla.
It is a known fact [25], that there exists a constant \alpha for any k, \mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}]\geq\alpha k^{-1/2}.
For any k, let \texttt{MAJORITY}^{\geq k}_{n} be the real-valued Boolean function obtained from \texttt{MAJORITY}_{n} by setting all Fourier coefficients of degree at most k to zero. Formally,
\displaystyle\texttt{MAJORITY}^{\geq k}_{n}(x):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq[n]\\
|S|\geq k\end{subarray}}\widehat{\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}}(S)\,\chi_{S}(x).
(48)
Similarly define \texttt{MAJORITY}^{<k}_{n}. Then, it holds that
\displaystyle\mathrm{corr}(f_{C},\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n})
\displaystyle=\mathrm{corr}(f_{C},\texttt{MAJORITY}^{\geq k}_{n})+\mathrm{corr}(f_{C},\texttt{MAJORITY}^{<k}_{n})
(49)
\displaystyle\leq\mathbf{W}^{<k}[f_{C}]^{1/2}\cdot\mathbf{W}^{<k}[\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}]^{1/2}
(50)
\displaystyle\qquad+\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]^{1/2}\cdot\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}]^{1/2}
(Cauchy-Schwarz)
\displaystyle\leq\mathbf{W}^{<k}[\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}]^{1/2}+\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]^{1/2}
(51)
\displaystyle\leq 1-\frac{\alpha}{2}k^{-1/2}+\mathbf{W}^{\geq k}[f_{C}]^{1/2}.
(52)
Also, \mathrm{corr}(f_{C},\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n})\geq 1-n^{-\delta}. Hence, for k^{\prime}=0.01\alpha^{2}n^{2\delta},
\displaystyle\mathbf{W}^{\geq k^{\prime}}[f_{C}]^{1/2}
\displaystyle\geq 0.5\alpha k^{\prime-1/2}-n^{-\delta}
(53)
\displaystyle=5\cdot n^{-\delta}-n^{-\delta}
(54)
\displaystyle=\Omega(n^{-\delta}).
(55)
Thus, \mathbf{W}^{\geq k^{\prime}}[f_{C}]=\Omega(n^{-2\delta}), and applying Corollary 4.2, this implies a O(1/\delta)=O(1) depth {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit for \texttt{PARITY}_{n}.
∎
This result also implies that a worst-case, approximate MAJORITY circuit can be made exact (due to FANOUT).
\hardworstmajority
Proof.
For each input, make k copies using \texttt{FANOUT}_{n} and run C in parallel. Then, compute \texttt{MAJORITY}_{k} of all the runs to output the final answer. From a standard Chernoff bound, k can be chosen to be {\mathsf{poly}}(1/\varepsilon)={\mathsf{polylog}}(n) to achieve at most 1/n worst case error, while implementing the \texttt{FANOUT}_{k},\texttt{MAJORITY}_{k} in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}. The resulting {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit has \geq(1-1/n)-correlation with MAJORITY, and therefore the rest of the argument follows from Section 2.3.
∎
4.2 Felinity and {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete states
Recall the notion of Felinity, restated below.
See 2.1
We will first show the two main properties of felinity that will be used in subsequent reductions. These are: (1) felinity behaves naturally under trace distance (Lemma 4.3) (2) a circuit for preparing an n-qubit \rho produces a circuit for \mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho) correlation with parity \texttt{PARITY}_{n} (Section 2.2).
Lemma 4.3 (Felinity is Lipschitz-continuous).
Let \rho,\sigma be n-qubit states. Then
|\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho)-\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\sigma)|\leq 8\,\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma),
where
\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma):=\frac{1}{2}\|\rho-\sigma\|_{1}.
Proof.
Consider the computational basis measurement on 2n-qubit states. For any \bm{y},\bm{z}\in\{0,1\}^{n} and a n-qubit state \rho^{\prime}, define,
\displaystyle q_{\rho^{\prime}}(\bm{y}\bm{z})
\displaystyle:=\braket{\bm{y},\bm{z}|\rho^{\prime}\otimes\rho^{\prime}|\bm{y},\bm{z}}=\braket{\bm{y}|\rho^{\prime}|\bm{y}}\braket{\bm{z}|\rho^{\prime}|\bm{z}}
(56)
This is precisely the probability of the measurement outcome \bm{y}\bm{z}\in\{0,1\}^{2n} on the 2n-qubit state \rho^{\prime}\otimes\rho^{\prime}. From triangle inequality and contractivity of trace distance under measurement,
\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{y},\bm{z}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\left\lvert q_{\rho}(\bm{y}\bm{z})-q_{\sigma}(\bm{y}\bm{z})\right\rvert
\displaystyle\leq\mathrm{TD}(\rho\otimes\rho,\sigma\otimes\sigma)
(57)
\displaystyle\leq 2\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma).
(58)
For \bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, let \overline{\bm{y}} be the string obtained by flipping all bits of \bm{y}, i.e, \ket{\overline{\bm{y}}}=X^{\otimes n}\ket{\bm{y}}. Then,
\displaystyle\left\lvert\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho)-\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\sigma)\right\rvert
\displaystyle=2\left\lvert\sum_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}q_{\rho}(\bm{y}\overline{\bm{y}})-q_{\sigma}(\bm{y}\overline{\bm{y}})\right\rvert
(59)
\displaystyle\leq 2\sum_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\left\lvert q_{\rho}(\bm{y}\overline{\bm{y}})-q_{\sigma}(\bm{y}\overline{\bm{y}})\right\rvert
(60)
\displaystyle\leq 2\sum_{\bm{y},\bm{z}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\left\lvert q_{\rho}(\bm{y}\bm{z})-q_{\sigma}(\bm{y}\bm{z})\right\rvert
(61)
\displaystyle\leq 8\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\sigma).
(62)
∎
Recall that we treat the output of the circuit as as a \pm 1 valued measurement outcome. Any Hermitian matrix \mathcal{O} is a valid observable corresponding to a measurement with possible outcomes among the eigenvalues of \mathcal{O}. For a state \ket{\psi}, the expected outcome of measuring \mathcal{O} on \ket{\psi} is given by \braket{\psi|\mathcal{O}|\psi}.
For n-input, m-ancillae {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C with a designated target t, define the following observable,
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{C}:=\bra{{\vec{0}}^{m}}_{A}\cdot{C^{\dagger}Z_{t}C}\cdot\ket{{\vec{0}}^{m}}_{A}
(63)
Physically, \mathcal{O}_{C} can be interpreted as the Heisenberg evolution of the output measurement. Mathematically, \mathcal{O}_{C} is simply a 2^{n}\times 2^{n} Hermitian matrix with eigenvalues in [-1,1] satisfying f_{C}({\bm{x}})=\braket{{\bm{x}}|\mathcal{O}_{C}|{\bm{x}}}.
With this formalism in mind, we proceed to show the main property of felinity.
\parfromfeln
Proof.
Let T=\left\{t_{1},t_{2}\dots t_{n}\right\} and A be the set of qubits (including T) of C. To construct C^{\prime}, first label the input qubits X=\left\{x_{1},x_{2}\dots x_{n}\right\} and define a layer of \mathtt{CZ} gates, L:=\bigotimes_{i\in[n]}\mathtt{CZ}(x_{i},t_{i}).Using a fresh ancilla a, designated as the target register, define the following reversible-\mathtt{NOR} gate,
\displaystyle G
\displaystyle:=(I-\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m})_{A}\otimes I_{a}+\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m}_{A}\otimes X_{a}
(64)
\displaystyle=I-2\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m}_{A}\otimes\outerproduct*{-}{-}_{a}
(65)
This gate flips the target a when the \mathtt{NOR} of all the controls is 1 and is a valid {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} gate. Then, C^{\prime} is given by,
\displaystyle C^{\prime}:=GC^{\dagger}LC
(66)
and is a depth 2d+2 circuit with m+1 ancillae.
We will now analyze the correlation of C^{\prime} with \texttt{PARITY}({\bm{x}}) as defined in Definition 3.4.
First define the observable \mathcal{O}_{C^{\prime}} corresponding to measurement outcome of C^{\prime}, s.t f_{C^{\prime}}=\braket{{\bm{x}}|\mathcal{O}_{C^{\prime}}|{\bm{x}}}
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{C^{\prime}}
\displaystyle=\braket{0^{m}_{A},0_{a}|(C^{\prime})^{\dagger}Z_{a}\otimes I_{A}C^{\prime}|0^{m}_{A},0_{a}}
(67)
\displaystyle=\braket{0^{m}_{A},0_{a}|C^{\dagger}LCG^{\dagger}Z_{a}GC^{\dagger}LC|0^{m}_{A},0_{a}}
\displaystyle\qquad(L=L^{\dagger})
(68)
\displaystyle=\braket{\psi_{A},0_{a}|LCG^{\dagger}Z_{a}GC^{\dagger}L|\psi_{A},0_{a}}
(69)
\displaystyle=\bra{\psi}_{A}\cdot LC\braket{0_{a}|G^{\dagger}Z_{a}G|0_{a}}C^{\dagger}L^{\dagger}\cdot\ket{\psi}_{A}
(70)
\displaystyle=\bra{\psi}_{A}\cdot LC(2\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m}-I)C^{\dagger}L^{\dagger}\cdot\ket{\psi}_{A}
(71)
\displaystyle=\bra{\psi}_{A}\cdot L(2\outerproduct*{\psi}{\psi}-I)L^{\dagger}\cdot\ket{\psi}_{A}
(72)
\displaystyle=2\bra{\psi}_{A}\cdot L\cdot\outerproduct*{\psi}{\psi}_{A}\cdot L\cdot\ket{\psi}_{A}-\bra{\psi}_{A}\cdot LL^{\dagger}\cdot\ket{\psi}_{A}
(73)
\displaystyle=\underbrace{2\bra{\psi}_{A}L\outerproduct*{\psi}{\psi}_{A}L\ket{\psi}_{A}}_{\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{C^{\prime}}}-I_{n}
(74)
In Eq. 70 we used the following derivation for the observable induced on A,X through Eq. 64
\displaystyle\bra{0_{a}}G^{\dagger}Z_{a}G\ket{0_{a}}
\displaystyle=\bra{0_{a}}G^{\dagger}\outerproduct*{0}{0}_{a}G\ket{0_{a}}-\bra{0_{a}}G^{\dagger}\outerproduct*{1}{1}_{a}G\ket{0_{a}}
(75)
\displaystyle=(\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m})\cdot(\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m})-(I-\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m})(I-\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m})
(76)
\displaystyle=\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m}-(I-\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m})
(77)
\displaystyle=(2\outerproduct*{0^m}{0^m}-I).
(78)
Next, we expand \ket{\psi} in the standard basis on T. We re-label each basis state \ket{\bm{y}}_{T}, for \bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n} by mapping to a unique subset S\subseteq[n] based on the 1 bits in \bm{y}. This associates each basis state with a Fourier character \chi_{S}, giving,
\displaystyle\ket{\psi}
\displaystyle=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\alpha_{S}\ket{S}\ket{\phi_{S}}_{A\setminus T}.
(79)
for some arbitrary states \ket{\phi_{S}} on the remaining ancillae and coefficients \alpha_{S}. Putting it together,
\displaystyle\varepsilon=\mathrm{corr}({f_{C^{\prime}},\texttt{PARITY}})
\displaystyle=\Ex_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}\braket{{\bm{x}}|\mathcal{O}_{C^{\prime}}|{\bm{x}}}(-1)^{|{\bm{x}}|}
(80)
\displaystyle=\Ex_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}\braket{{\bm{x}}|\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{C^{\prime}}|{\bm{x}}}(-1)^{|{\bm{x}}|}{\ -\Ex_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}(-1)^{|{\bm{x}}|}}
(81)
\displaystyle=2\cdot\Ex_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}\braket{\psi,{\bm{x}}|L|\psi}\braket{\psi|L|\psi,{\bm{x}}}(-1)^{|{\bm{x}}|}
(82)
\displaystyle=2\sum_{S,S^{\prime}\subseteq[n]}\alpha^{*}_{S}\alpha_{S^{\prime}}\cdot\Ex_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}\braket{S,\phi_{S},{\bm{x}}|L|\psi}\braket{\psi|L|S^{\prime},\phi_{S^{\prime}},{\bm{x}}}\chi_{[n]}({\bm{x}})
(83)
\displaystyle=2\sum_{S,S^{\prime}\subseteq[n]}\alpha^{*}_{S}\alpha_{S^{\prime}}\cdot\Ex_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}\chi_{S}({\bm{x}})\chi_{S^{\prime}}({\bm{x}})\braket{S,\phi_{S}|\psi}\braket{\psi|S^{\prime},\phi_{S^{\prime}}}\chi_{[n]}({\bm{x}})
(84)
\displaystyle=2\sum_{S,S^{\prime}\subseteq[n]}\left\lvert\alpha_{S}\right\rvert^{2}\left\lvert\alpha_{S^{\prime}}\right\rvert^{2}\cdot\Ex_{{\bm{x}}\sim\{0,1\}^{n}}\chi_{S\Delta S^{\prime}}({\bm{x}})\chi_{[n]}({\bm{x}})
(85)
\displaystyle=2\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\left\lvert\alpha_{S}\right\rvert^{2}\left\lvert\alpha_{\overline{S}}\right\rvert^{2}.
(86)
Observe that \left\lvert\alpha_{S}\right\rvert^{2}=\braket{S|\rho_{T}|S}, for \rho_{T}=\tr_{A\setminus T}\outerproduct*{\psi}{\psi}.
Mapping the labels S back to bit-strings gives,
\displaystyle\mathrm{corr}({f_{C^{\prime}},\texttt{PARITY}})
\displaystyle=2\sum_{\bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\braket{\bm{y}|\rho_{T}|\bm{y}}\braket{\bm{y}|X^{\otimes n}\cdot\rho_{T}\cdot X^{\otimes n}|\bm{y}}
(87)
\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\rho_{T}).
(88)
∎
We conclude with the following reduction.
\felntofanout
Proof.
This follows directly from Section 2.2 and Section 2.1.1.
∎
4.2.1 Poly weight Dicke states are {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-complete
It is known that any Dicke state \ket{D^{k}_{n}} can be constructed in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}, i.e using \texttt{FANOUT}_{n}. We will show that constructing \ket{D^{k}_{n}} in constant depth requires \texttt{FANOUT}_{\min(k,n-k)}.
Definition 4.4 (Uniform k-hamming slice / Dicke \mathcal{D}^{n}_{k}).
The uniform distribution on all n-bit strings of hamming weight k. The associated state is \ket{D^{n}_{k}}, the n-qubit k-weight Dicke state,
\ket{D^{n}_{k}}:=\binom{n}{k}^{-1/2}\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^{n},|b|=k}\ket{b}.
We will focus on k\leq n/2 WLOG, since \ket{D^{n-k}_{n}} has the same complexity as \ket{D^{n}_{k}}.
Fact 4.5 (Binomial distribution bounds [14]).
For any sufficiently large n\in\mathbb{N}, and any k\leq n/2
\Pr[\mathsf{Binom}(n,k/n)=k]\geq\frac{e^{-1}}{\sqrt{k}}
To prove {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-completeness of Dicke state preparation, we first prove the following reduction from Dicke states to non-negligible felinity states.
Lemma 4.6.
For any n and k\leq n/2, there is a single layer L of {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} gates acting on n+\ell qubits for \ell=\lfloor k/\log k\rfloor, such that, the state
\ket{\psi}=L\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\ket{0^{\ell}}_{T} satisfies,
\mathcal{F}_{{}_{\ell}}\left(\tr_{\overline{T}}\outerproduct*{\psi}{\psi}\right)\geq\frac{1}{8k}.
Proof.
