Partition the qubits into \ell=\lfloor k/\log k\rfloor blocks. Let B_{i} be the m_{i}=|B_{i}|\geq n/\ell qubits in each block, and label a corresponding qubit of T as t_{i}.
Let p=\frac{k}{n}. Then, L is given by,
\displaystyle L
\displaystyle=\bigotimes_{i\in[\ell]}(I_{B_{i}}-\outerproduct*{p}{p}^{\otimes m_{i}}\otimes\outerproduct*{+}{+}_{t_{i}})
(89)
\displaystyle=\bigotimes_{i\in[\ell]}\left[(I_{B_{i}}-\outerproduct*{p}{p}^{\otimes m_{i}})\otimes I_{t_{i}}+\outerproduct*{p}{p}^{\otimes m_{i}}\otimes X_{t_{i}}\right].
(90)
As described in Eq. 90, each gate can be viewed as a controlled-not gate, that flips t_{i} whenever B_{i} lies in the \outerproduct*{p}{p}^{\otimes m_{i}} subspace.
Now, for \ket{\psi}=L\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\ket{0^{\ell}}, we will first argue that \left\lVert\bra{1^{\ell}}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq\varepsilon and \left\lVert\bra{0^{\ell}}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}\geq\varepsilon. From Eq. 90, we have,
\displaystyle\left\lVert\bra{1^{\ell}}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}
\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bra{p}^{\otimes n}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}
(91)
\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bra{p}^{\otimes n}\cdot\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rVert^{2}
(92)
\displaystyle=\Pr\left[\mathsf{Binom}(n,p)=k\right]
(93)
\displaystyle\geq\frac{e^{-1}}{\sqrt{k}}.\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\text{(from \lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{fact:binombounds})}
(94)
similarly, letting \Pi=\bigotimes_{i\in[\ell]}(I-\outerproduct*{p}{p}^{\otimes m_{i}}),
\displaystyle\left\lVert\bra{0^{\ell}}_{T}\cdot\ket{\psi}\right\rVert^{2}
\displaystyle=\left\lVert\Pi\cdot\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rVert^{2}.
(95)
Instead of directly bounding \left\lVert\Pi\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rVert^{2}, we bound \left\lvert\braket{\nu|D^{n}_{k}}\right\rvert^{2} for a vector \ket{\nu} that is nearly a +1 eigenvector of \Pi. Define, \ket{p_{-}}=\sqrt{1-p}\ket{0}-\sqrt{p}\ket{1}.
Observe that, for each i,
\displaystyle\braket{p_{-}|p}^{2m_{i}}
\displaystyle=(1-2p)^{2m_{i}}
(96)
\displaystyle\leq\exp(-4k/\ell)
(97)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k^{4}}.
(98)
Therefore,
\displaystyle\left\lVert\Pi\ket{p_{-}}^{\otimes n}\right\rVert^{2}
\displaystyle=\prod_{i\in[\ell]}(1-\left\lvert\braket{p|p_{-}}\right\rvert^{2m_{i}})
(99)
\displaystyle\geq\left(1-1/k^{4}\right)^{\ell}
(100)
\displaystyle\geq 1-1/k^{3}.
(101)
Therefore, \ket{p_{-}}^{\otimes n} is nearly an eigenvector of \Pi, and,
\displaystyle\left\lVert\Pi\cdot\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rVert
\displaystyle\geq\left\lvert\bra{p_{-}}^{\otimes n}\cdot\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rvert-1/k^{3/2}
(102)
\displaystyle=\left\lVert\bra{p}^{\otimes n}\cdot Z^{\otimes n}\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rVert-1/k^{3/2}
(103)
\displaystyle=\left\lVert(-1)^{k}\cdot\bra{p}^{\otimes n}\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rVert-1/k^{3/2}
(104)
\displaystyle=\sqrt{\Pr\left[\mathsf{Binom}(n,p)=k\right]}-1/k^{3/2}
(105)
\displaystyle\geq\frac{e^{-1.01}}{k^{1/4}}.
(106)
Hence, \left\lVert\Pi\cdot\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\right\rVert^{2}\gtrsim 1/\sqrt{k}.
Combining with Eq. 95 and Eq. 94, for \rho_{T}=\tr_{\overline{T}}\outerproduct*{\psi}{\psi},
\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{{}_{\ell}}(\rho_{T})
\displaystyle\geq\braket{0^{\ell}|\rho_{T}|0^{\ell}}\braket{1^{\ell}|\rho_{T}|1^{\ell}}
(107)
\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{8k}.\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\text{(using $e^{2.01}\approx 7.5$)}
(108)
∎
Now we prove the {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}_{f}-completeness of poly-weight Dicke states.
\dicketocat
Proof.
Consider the circuit C from Lemma 4.6, and let \sigma^{*}, \sigma be the state on the \ell=\lfloor k/\log k\rfloor-qubit register T after applying C to \ket{D^{n}_{k}}\ket{0^{\ell}}_{T} and \rho\otimes\outerproduct*{0^{\ell}}{0^{\ell}}_{T} respectively.
Then,
\displaystyle\mathrm{TD}(\sigma,\sigma^{*})
\displaystyle\leq\mathrm{TD}(\rho\otimes\outerproduct*{0^{\ell}}{0^{\ell}},\ket{D^{n}_{k}}\ket{0^{\ell}})
(109)
\displaystyle=\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\ket{D^{n}_{k}}).
(110)
Then, from Lemma 4.3,
\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{{}_{\ell}}(\sigma)
\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{8k}-8\mathrm{TD}(\rho,\ket{D^{n}_{k}})
(111)
\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{8k}-\frac{1}{10k}
(112)
\displaystyle=\Omega(1/k).
(113)
By Section 2.2, this implies a depth O(d), m\cdot{\mathsf{poly}}(n)-ancilla circuit for \texttt{FANOUT}_{\ell}. Note \log\ell/\log k=1-o(1). Then, using the recursive nature of FANOUT [23, 27], this provides a depth d^{\prime}=O(d), m^{\prime}=m\cdot{\mathsf{poly}}(n)-ancilla circuit for \texttt{FANOUT}_{k}, as well as a depth O(d^{\prime}/\delta), O(m^{\prime}n^{1-\delta}) ancillae circuit for \texttt{FANOUT}_{n}.
∎
\polydickeisfanout
Proof.
Either \rho or X^{\otimes n}\rho is within 1/k trace distance of \ket{D^{n}_{k}}. Since \log k/\log n=\Theta(1), Section 2.2.1 implies a O(1) depth and {\mathsf{poly}}(n) ancilla circuit for \texttt{FANOUT}_{n}.
∎
5 Upper bounds for {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}
We now prove some important building blocks for our construction of a circuit with high MAJORITY correlation. We will first show that “poor-man’s fanout” lies in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, and then combine this with a “weak-copy” test, which estimates the hamming weight of the original string these weak copies were made from.
The “poor-mans fanout” circuit is an upgraded version of a controlled-W map, which we use in its implementation.
Claim 5.1 (Uniform 0^{n} and W_{n}).
For any n, the state \ket{W^{\prime}_{n}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{0^{n}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{W_{n}} can be cleanly prepared in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} using O(n) qubits.
Proof.
Start with the state \ket{\psi_{0}}_{T}:=\ket{1/p}^{\otimes n} for p=1/(n+1). Observe that,
\displaystyle p_{1}:=\Pr_{x\sim\mathsf{Bern}(1/{n+1},n)}\left[|x|=1\right]
\displaystyle=n\cdot(p)\cdot(1-p)^{n}
(114)
\displaystyle=(1-p)^{n}
(115)
\displaystyle=\Pr_{x\sim\mathsf{Bern}(1/{n+1},n)}\left[|x|=0\right].
(116)
Then, applying the \texttt{THRESHOLD}^{n}_{1}, which is in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}, onto a new ancilla a, we can prepare,
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{1}}_{T,a}
\displaystyle=\texttt{THRESHOLD}^{n}_{1}\ket{\psi_{0}}_{T}\ket{0}_{a}
(117)
\displaystyle=\sqrt{p_{1}}\ket{W^{\prime}_{n}}_{T}\ket{1}_{a}+\sqrt{1-p_{1}}\ket{\mathrm{bad}}_{T}\ket{0}_{a}.
(118)
From known binomial bounds (see Fact 4.5), \lim_{n\to\infty}p_{1}=e^{-1}\approx 0.367. Hence p_{1}\geq 1/4 and applying Claim 3.9 produces \ket{W^{\prime}_{n}} cleanly.
∎
Lemma 5.2 (Controlled W map).
We can apply the following map cleanly in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}:
\ket{0}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}\mapsto\ket{0}_{x}\ket{0^{n}},\quad\ket{1}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}\mapsto\ket{1}_{x}\ket{W_{n}}.
Proof.
One can construct the following state using an \mathtt{OR} gate, then an additional XZ gate on qubit x from Claim 5.1.
\displaystyle\ket{\varphi}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{1}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{0}_{x}\ket{W_{n}}.
(119)
We can implement {\mathsf{R}}_{\varphi}=(I-2\outerproduct*{\varphi}{\varphi}), the reflection about this state in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} using Fact 3.6. This has the effect of swapping the two branches.
Then, on input b\in\{0,1\}, first construct the state, using Claim 5.1.
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{0}(b)}
\displaystyle:=\ket{b}_{x}\ket{W^{\prime}_{n}}
(120)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{b}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{b}_{x}\ket{W_{n}}
(121)
Next, apply {\mathsf{R}}_{\varphi} to obtain \ket{\psi_{1}(b)}. Observe that when b=1, we have,
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{1}(1)}
\displaystyle:={\mathsf{R}}_{\varphi}\ket{\psi_{0}(1)}
(122)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left({\mathsf{R}}_{\varphi}\ket{1}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}\right)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{1}_{x}\ket{W_{n}}
(123)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{0}_{x}\ket{W_{n}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{1}_{x}\ket{W_{n}}
(124)
\displaystyle=\ket{+}_{x}\ket{W_{n}}
(125)
Because the \ket{1}\ket{W_{n}} branch is orthogonal to \ket{\varphi}.
Similarly, when b=0, we obtain the state \ket{\psi_{1}(0)}=\ket{+}_{x}\ket{0^{n}}. To make this map clean, we can apply an H gate on x and then another \mathtt{OR} gate to recover the input value of b.
∎
Corollary 5.3 (Any superposition of \ket{0^{n}}, \ket{W_{n}}).
For any \alpha,\beta such that \left\lvert\alpha\right\rvert^{2}+\left\lvert\beta\right\rvert^{2}=1, we can prepare the state,
\ket{W_{n}(\alpha,\beta)}:=\alpha\ket{0^{n}}+\beta\ket{W_{n}} in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.
Proof.
To prepare the desired superposition, start with a qubit \ket{\nu}_{x}=\alpha\ket{0}+\beta\ket{1} and apply the circuit from Lemma 5.2. To uncompute qubit x apply an \mathtt{OR} gate.
∎
5.1 Poor man’s fanout
Lemma 5.4 (Uncompute \ket{W_{n}} but not \ket{0^{n}}).
There is a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C that cleanly achieves the mapping,
C\ket{1/n}^{\otimes n}\ket{1}=\ket{W^{n}}\ket{1}\qquad\text{and}\qquad C\ket{0^{n}}\ket{0}=\ket{0^{n}}\ket{0}
Proof.
First we will describe a circuit C_{0} to go from \ket{1/n}^{\otimes n}\ket{1} to \ket{W}\ket{1}. Then we will argue that C_{0} acts as desired on \ket{0}\ket{0}. First using a fresh ancilla, a_{0}, obtain,
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{1}}
\displaystyle:=\texttt{EXACT}_{1}(X,a_{0})\ket{1/n}^{\otimes n}_{X}\ket{1}_{q}\ket{0}_{a_{0}}
(126)
\displaystyle=\sqrt{p}\ket{W_{n}}\ket{1}_{q}\ket{1}_{a_{0}}+\sqrt{1-p}\ket{\mathrm{bad}}\ket{1}_{q}\ket{0}_{a_{0}}.
(127)
where p=\Pr[\mathsf{Binom}(1/n,n)=1]\geq e^{-1}. Then, similar to Claim 3.9, apply a controlled-\mathrm{Rot}_{\gamma} gate controlled on both q and a_{0} to obtain,
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{2}}
\displaystyle:=\text{cc-}\mathrm{Rot}_{\gamma}(q,a_{0},a_{1})\ket{\psi_{1}}\ket{0}_{a_{1}}
(128)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\ket{W_{n}}\ket{1}_{q}\ket{1}_{a_{0}}\ket{1}_{a_{1}}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\ket{\mathrm{bad}}_{T,q,a_{0}}\ket{0}_{a_{1}}.
(129)
Let {\mathsf{R}}_{\ket{\psi_{2}}}:=(I-2\outerproduct*{\psi_2}{\psi_2}) be the reflection about \ket{\psi_{2}}.
Observe that since \ket{\psi_{2}} can be constructed in O(1) depth, {\mathsf{R}}_{\ket{\psi_{2}}} is also in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.
Next, obtain,
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{3}}
\displaystyle:=Z_{a_{0}}{\mathsf{R}}_{\ket{\psi_{2}}}Z_{a_{0}}\ket{\psi_{2}}
(130)
\displaystyle=-Z_{a_{0}}{\mathsf{R}}_{\ket{\psi_{2}}}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\ket{W_{n}}\ket{1}_{q}\ket{1}_{a_{0}}\ket{1}_{a_{1}}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\ket{\mathrm{bad}}_{T,q,a_{0}}\ket{0}_{a_{1}}\right)
(131)
\displaystyle=-Z_{a_{0}}\ket{W_{n}}\ket{1}_{q}\ket{1}_{a_{0}}\ket{1}_{a_{1}}
(132)
\displaystyle=\ket{W_{n}}\ket{1}_{q}\ket{1}_{a_{0}}\ket{1}_{a_{1}}.
(133)
On input registers marked X,q and ancillae \ket{00}_{a_{0},a_{1}}, this circuit is given by,
\displaystyle C_{0}:=Z_{a_{0}}{\mathsf{R}}_{\ket{\psi_{2}}}Z_{a_{0}}\cdot\text{cc-}\mathrm{Rot}_{\gamma}\cdot\texttt{EXACT}_{1}(X,a_{0}).
(134)
Then, observe that all these gates are ineffective on input \ket{0^{n}}_{X}\ket{0}_{q}. In particular, \ket{\psi_{2}} is orthogonal to \ket{0^{n}}_{X}\ket{0^{3}}_{q,a_{0},a_{1}}. Therefore,
\displaystyle C_{0}\cdot\ket{0^{n}}_{X}\ket{0}_{q}\ket{00}_{a_{0},a_{1}}=\ket{0^{n}}_{X}\ket{0}_{q}\ket{00}_{a_{0},a_{1}}
(135)
\displaystyle C_{0}\cdot\ket{1/n}^{\otimes n}_{X}\ket{1}_{q}\ket{00}_{a_{0},a_{1}}=\ket{W_{n}}_{X}\ket{1}_{q}\ket{11}_{a_{0},a_{1}}
(136)
Thus, C:=\mathtt{CNOT}(q,a_{0})\mathtt{CNOT}(q,a_{1})C_{0} implements the desired mapping.
∎
Then, the reverse circuit for the above is our “poor man’s” n-fanout.
\poormansfanoutmap
Proof.
Let C be the circuit from Lemma 5.4. Then, this mapping is achieved by C^{\dagger}.
∎
5.2 Majority
For ease of description we will use the following claim formally connecting classical post-processing with limited fanout to {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuits.
Claim 5.5 (Closure under {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} postprocessing).
Let U be a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit that, on input {\bm{x}}, produces output qubits whose computational-basis measurement outcomes form a distribution \mathcal{D}({\bm{x}}) over \{0,1\}^{m(n)}. Suppose there is an {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuit T with {\mathsf{polylog}}(n) fanout satisfying, for all {\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n},
\Pr_{\bm{y}\sim\mathcal{D}({\bm{x}})}[T(\bm{y}))=g({\bm{x}})]\geq 1-\delta
for a function g({\bm{x}}), then there is a {\mathsf{poly}}(m) size single-output {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C (Definition 3.1) such that,
\mathrm{corr}(f_{C},g)\geq 1-2\delta.
Proof.
Using Fact 3.7, there is a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C^{\prime} acting on m inputs that, using {\mathsf{poly}}(m) ancillae, implements the following map for all \bm{y}\in\{0,1\}^{m},
\displaystyle\ket{\bm{y}}_{X}\ket{0}_{t}\mapsto\ket{\bm{y}}_{X}\ket{T(\bm{y})}_{t}
(137)
Now, observe that any measurement on the X register in the output does not affect measurements on the t register (since they commute). Prepend U to C^{\prime}, so that the m output qubits of U, feed into the inputs of C^{\prime} to obtain C that acts on n inputs.
Then, on any input {\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, apply C and measure both t and X in the standard basis. The distribution on t is exactly the one obtained by applying T(\bm{y}) on a sample from \mathcal{D}({\bm{x}}).
Thus the resulting circuit outputs g({\bm{x}}) with probability at least 1-\delta(n) on every input, which corresponds to correlation 1-2\delta(n) with g({\bm{x}}).
∎
Poor man’s fanout allows us to create n “weaker” copies of the input. In order to approximate majority, we can separately apply {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuits to each copy to estimate majority and amplify. A gadget with similar properties to poor man’s fanout was given in Appendix B of [12]. The lemma below, which will serve as the key ingredient in our test, is analogous to their Claim 28.
\oneweakcopytest
Proof.
Let \ket{\phi}:=a\ket{0^{n}}+b\ket{W_{n}} for some a,b with a^{2}+b^{2}=1 we will choose later, and let {\mathsf{R}}=(I-2\outerproduct*{\phi}{\phi}), the reflection about \ket{\phi}. Then, the circuit C first applies {\mathsf{R}} and then a \mathtt{OR} gate with o as the target. Mathematically, C is given by,
\displaystyle C:=(I-2\outerproduct*{0^n}{0^n}\otimes\outerproduct*{+}{+}_{o})\cdot{\mathsf{R}}
(138)
From Corollary 5.3 one can implement any such \ket{\phi} therefore implement {\mathsf{R}} using Fact 3.6 in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.
We will choose a,b as follows. First observe for any {\bm{x}}
of hamming weight \ell, \alpha_{\ell}:=\braket{0^{n}|\psi({\bm{x}})} and \gamma_{\ell}:=\braket{W_{n}|\psi({\bm{x}})} depend only on \ell.
Let s:=\sqrt{\alpha_{t}^{2}+\gamma_{t}^{2}}, observe s^{2} is the total weight on the subspace spanned by \ket{0^{n}},\ket{W_{n}} in \ket{\psi({\bm{x}})} whenever |{\bm{x}}|=t. Choose,
\displaystyle a=\sqrt{\frac{s-\gamma_{t}}{2s}},\qquad b=\sqrt{\frac{s+\gamma_{t}}{2s}}
(139)
so that 1-2a^{2}=\gamma_{t}/s and 2ab=\alpha_{t}/s.
This defines the circuit C through Eq. 138.
Now consider any input {\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n} and let \ell=|{\bm{x}}|. Then,
\ket{\psi({\bm{x}})} can be written as,
\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{\ell}}=\alpha_{\ell}\ket{0^{n}}+\gamma_{\ell}\ket{W_{n}}+\ket{\overline{\eta({\bm{x}})}}
(140)
for some un-normalized \ket{\overline{\eta({\bm{x}})}} with \braket{0^{n}|\overline{\eta({\bm{x}})}}=\braket{W_{n}|\overline{\eta({\bm{x}})}}.
Since the final \mathtt{OR} gate flips the ancilla o only in the subspace spanned by \ket{0^{n}}, the probability of measuring \ket{1} on the output is, \braket{1|\rho({\bm{x}})|1}=\left\lvert\braket{0^{n}|{\mathsf{R}}|\psi({\bm{x}})}\right\rvert^{2}, where,
\displaystyle\braket{0^{n}|{\mathsf{R}}|\psi({\bm{x}})}
\displaystyle=\bra{0^{n}}\cdot(I-2\outerproduct*{\phi}{\phi})\ket{\psi({\bm{x}})}
(141)
\displaystyle=2\bra{0^{n}}\cdot\outerproduct*{\phi}{\phi}\cdot\left(\gamma_{\ell}\ket{W_{n}}+\ket{\overline{\eta}({\bm{x}})}\right)+\alpha_{\ell}\braket{0^{n}|{\mathsf{R}}|0^{n}}
(142)
\displaystyle=2\gamma_{\ell}\bra{0^{n}}\cdot\outerproduct*{\phi}{\phi}\cdot\ket{W_{n}}+\alpha_{\ell}\braket{0^{n}|{\mathsf{R}}|0^{n}}
(143)
\displaystyle=2\gamma_{\ell}ab+\alpha_{\ell}\cdot(1-2a^{2})
(144)
\displaystyle=\gamma_{\ell}\cdot\alpha_{t}/s+\alpha_{\ell}\cdot\gamma_{t}/s
(145)
Now, letting r:=\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{n}}, gives \alpha_{\ell}=r^{\ell}.
Observing there are exactly \ell hamming weight 1 basis vectors with non-zero amplitudes of \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}r^{\ell-1} in \ket{\psi({\bm{x}})} gives \gamma_{\ell}=\frac{\ell}{n}r^{\ell-1}.
Substituting,
\displaystyle s
\displaystyle=\sqrt{r^{2t}+\frac{t^{2}}{n^{2}}r^{2t-2}}
(146)
\displaystyle=r^{t-1}\sqrt{r^{2}+\frac{t^{2}}{n^{2}}}
(147)
gives,
\displaystyle\braket{0^{n}|{\mathsf{R}}|\psi({\bm{x}})}=\frac{t-\ell}{n}\cdot\frac{r^{\ell}}{\sqrt{r^{2}+\frac{t^{2}}{n^{2}}}}.
(148)
Now assume |\ell-t|=O(\sqrt{n}\,{\mathsf{polylog}}n). Then (\ell-t)/n=o(1), hence
r^{\ell}=r^{t}(1+o(1)). Therefore
\displaystyle\braket{1|\rho({\bm{x}})|1}=(1+o(1))\left(\frac{\ell-t}{n}\right)^{2}\frac{r^{2t}}{r^{2}+\frac{t^{2}}{n^{2}}}.
(149)
Since r^{2t}=(1-\frac{1}{n})^{t}=e^{-t/n}(1+o(1)) and
r^{2}+\frac{t^{2}}{n^{2}}=1+\frac{t^{2}}{n^{2}}+o(1), it follows that
\displaystyle\braket{1|\rho({\bm{x}})|1}=\lambda_{t}(1+o(1))\left(\frac{\ell-t}{n}\right)^{2},\qquad\lambda_{t}:=\frac{e^{-t/n}}{1+t^{2}/n^{2}}=\Theta(1).
(150)
Therefore, as claimed,
\displaystyle\braket{0|\rho({\bm{x}})|0}
\displaystyle=1-\braket{1|\rho({\bm{x}})|1}=1-\lambda_{t}(1+o(1))\left(\frac{\ell-t}{n}\right)^{2}.
(151)
∎
Lemma 5.6 ({\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit for \texttt{APPROX}_{t}).
Let a={\mathsf{polylog}}(n) and let t\in\{0,\dots,n\}. There exists a {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit C such that, on every input {\bm{x}}\in\{0,1\}^{n} of Hamming weight \ell, C outputs 1 with probability at least 1-1/n if |\ell-t|<\frac{\sqrt{n}}{2a}, and outputs 0 with probability at least 1-1/n if |\ell-t|>\frac{\sqrt{n}}{a}.
Proof.
Let C_{0} be the circuit from Section 2.3.1, and let Z be the bit that is 1 iff the last qubit of C_{0} measures to \ket{1}. By Section 2.3.1, \Pr[Z=1]=\lambda_{t}(1+o(1))((\ell-t)/n)^{2}, where \lambda_{t}=\frac{e^{-t/n}}{1+t^{2}/n^{2}}. Thus, for all large enough n, we may bound the 1+o(1) factor between 2/3 and 4/3, so
\frac{2}{3}\lambda_{t}\left(\frac{\ell-t}{n}\right)^{2}\leq\Pr[Z=1]\leq\frac{4}{3}\lambda_{t}\left(\frac{\ell-t}{n}\right)^{2}.
Hence \Pr[Z=1]\leq\lambda_{t}/(3na^{2}) when |\ell-t|<\frac{\sqrt{n}}{2a}, and \Pr[Z=1]\geq 2\lambda_{t}/(3na^{2}) when |\ell-t|>\frac{\sqrt{n}}{a}.
Set r=\lceil 3na^{2}/\lambda_{t}\rceil, m=d\log n for a large enough constant d, and s=\lceil rm/n\rceil={\mathsf{polylog}}(n). Using {\mathsf{polylog}}(n) fanout, make s copies of the input string {\bm{x}}. For each copied string and each i\in[n], apply Section 2.3.1 to the copied bit x_{i}. For each u\in[n], the uth fanout outputs across i=1,\dots,n form one copy of the encoded input \ket{x_{1}/n}\cdots\ket{x_{n}/n}. Thus we obtain sn\geq rm unentangled encoded inputs, and hence rm independent copies Z_{j,k} of Z, with j\in[m] and k\in[r].
Let W_{j}=\bigvee_{k=1}^{r}Z_{j,k}. In the first case, \Pr[W_{j}=1]\leq r\Pr[Z=1]\leq 2/3. In the second,
\Pr[W_{j}=1]=1-(1-\Pr[Z=1])^{r}\geq 1-\left(1-\frac{2\lambda_{t}}{3na^{2}}\right)^{r}\geq 1-e^{-2}.
Since the W_{j} are independent, a Chernoff bound gives \sum_{j}W_{j}<0.7m in the first case and \sum_{j}W_{j}>0.8m in the second, each with probability at least 1-1/n, for large enough d.
By a well-known result of Ajtai and Ben-Or [2], there is an approximate-majority function on m bits, that is, a function A_{m}:\{0,1\}^{m}\to\{0,1\} computable by an {\mathsf{AC}}^{0} circuit of size {\mathsf{poly}}(m), which outputs 1 whenever the input Hamming weight is below 0.7m and outputs 0 whenever it is above 0.8m. Since m=O(\log n), this circuit has size, and hence fanout, at most {\mathsf{polylog}}(n). Applying A_{m} to W_{1},\dots,W_{m} therefore gives the desired output with probability at least 1-1/n, and the result follows from Claim 5.5.
∎
\ezmajority
Proof.
Let \gamma=\frac{\sqrt{n}}{a} and \eta=\frac{\sqrt{n}}{2a}. For each threshold t, let D_{t} be the {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0} circuit from Lemma 5.6 . Thus, on inputs of Hamming weight \ell, D_{t} outputs 1 with probability at least 1-1/n if |\ell-t|<\eta, and outputs 0 with probability at least 1-1/n if |\ell-t|>\gamma.
Let L=c^{\prime}\log{n}\sqrt{n} for a sufficiently large constant c^{\prime}, and consider thresholds
T_{+}=\{n/2+j\eta:1\leq j\leq L/\eta\},\qquad T_{-}=\{n/2-j\eta:1\leq j\leq L/\eta\}.
Since |T_{+}\cup T_{-}|={\mathsf{polylog}}(n), we may run all the circuits D_{t} in parallel. Let C output 1 if some D_{t} with t\in T_{+} outputs 1, output 0 if some D_{t} with t\in T_{-} outputs 1, and output an arbitrary bit otherwise. By Claim 5.5, this is computable in {\mathsf{QAC}}^{0}.
If \gamma<\ell-n/2\leq L, then some t\in T_{+} satisfies |\ell-t|<\eta, while every t\in T_{-} satisfies |\ell-t|>\gamma. Hence, except with probability at most |T_{+}\cup T_{-}|/n, the circuit C outputs 1=\texttt{MAJORITY}_{n}(x). The case -L\leq\ell-n/2<-\gamma is symmetric.
Thus C can disagree with \texttt{MAJORITY}_{n} only if one of the above tests outputs the wrong answer, if |\ell-n/2|\leq\gamma, or if |\ell-n/2|>L. The first case contributes at most |T_{+}\cup T_{-}|/n={\mathsf{polylog}}(n)/n failure probability. To analyze the second case, for a uniformly random input, the probability that the hamming weight \ell satisfies |\ell-n/2|\leq\gamma is at most O(\gamma/\sqrt{n})=O(1/a). For the last case, the probability that \ell satisfies |\ell-n/2|>L is at most 2e^{-2L^{2}/n}=O(1/n). Each of these contributions is O(1/a). Therefore C agrees with \texttt{MAJORITY}_{n} on a 1-O(1/a) fraction of inputs, and hence has correlation at least 1-1/a after adjusting constants.
∎

Appendix A Skipped proofs
See 3.5
Proof of Claim 3.5.
Preserve the input registers by making a classical copy of each input coordinate x_{i} in a single layer of \mathtt{CNOT} gates at the start. This increases the number of ancillae to a=n+m. Call this circuit C_{0}. Let A be the set of ancilla qubits of C_{0} other than output register t, then, wlog, the final state of C_{0} has the form,
\displaystyle C_{0}\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{0^{a}}_{t,A}
\displaystyle=\ket{{\bm{x}}}\left(\sqrt{p_{0}({\bm{x}})}\ket{0}_{t}\ket{\psi_{0}({\bm{x}})}_{A}+\sqrt{p_{1}({\bm{x}})}\ket{1}_{t}\ket{\psi_{1}({\bm{x}})}_{A}\right)
(152)
for some arbitrary input-dependent states \ket{\psi_{0}({\bm{x}})} and \ket{\psi_{1}({\bm{x}})} on the remaining ancillae that contain global phases to absorb the additional phases. Now using another fresh ancilla t^{\prime}, define C^{\prime} using the standard copy-uncompute procedure as,
\displaystyle C^{\prime}:=C_{0}^{\dagger}\cdot\mathtt{CNOT}(t,t^{\prime})\cdot C_{0}
(153)
Then,
\displaystyle\mathtt{CNOT}(t,t^{\prime})C_{0}\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{0^{a}}_{A}\ket{0}_{t^{\prime}}
\displaystyle=\ket{{\bm{x}}}\underbrace{\left(\sqrt{p_{0}({\bm{x}})}\ket{0}_{t}\ket{\psi_{0}({\bm{x}})}_{A}\ket{0}_{t^{\prime}}+\sqrt{p_{1}({\bm{x}})}\ket{1}_{t}\ket{\psi_{1}({\bm{x}})}_{A}\ket{1}_{t^{\prime}}\right)}_{\ket{\varphi({\bm{x}})}}.
(154)
Therefore, for both values of \bm{b}\in\{0,1\}, the claimed amplitude is,
\displaystyle\alpha_{b}({\bm{x}})
\displaystyle:=\bra{{\bm{x}}}\bra{0^{a}}\bra{b}_{t^{\prime}}\cdot C^{\prime}\cdot\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{0^{a+1}}_{A,t^{\prime}}
(155)
\displaystyle=\left(\bra{{\bm{x}}}\bra{0^{a}}\bra{b}_{t^{\prime}}\cdot C_{0}^{\dagger}\right)\cdot\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{\varphi({\bm{x}})}_{A,t^{\prime}}
(156)
\displaystyle=\left(\bra{{\bm{x}}}\bra{0^{a}}\bra{b}_{t^{\prime}}\cdot C_{0}^{\dagger}\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{p_{b}({\bm{x}})}\cdot\ket{{\bm{x}}}\ket{b}_{t}\ket{b}_{t^{\prime}}\ket{\psi_{b}({\bm{x}})}_{A}\right)
(157)
\displaystyle=\left(\sqrt{p_{0}({\bm{x}})}\bra{0}_{t}\bra{\psi_{0}({\bm{x}})}_{A}+\sqrt{p_{1}({\bm{x}})}\bra{1}_{t}\bra{\psi_{1}({\bm{x}})}\right)_{A}\cdot\sqrt{p_{b}({\bm{x}})}\ket{b}_{t}\ket{\psi_{b}({\bm{x}})}_{A}
(158)
\displaystyle=p_{b}({\bm{x}}).
(159)
∎
Lemma A.1 (Felinity of uniformly rotated W states).
For any state \ket{\psi} of the form \ket{\psi}:=U^{\otimes n}\ket{W_{n}} for any unitary U,
\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\psi)=\mathrm{negl}(n).
Proof.
U can be written in its Euler angle decomposition as,
\displaystyle U=e^{i\delta}R_{z}(\alpha)R_{y}(\beta)R_{z}(\gamma).
(160)
Observe that any global phases and any matrices that commute with Z do not affect the felinity, since it is defined with respect to Z-basis measurements. Therefore, all the R_{z} rotations commute and it suffices to analyze R_{y}(\beta), i.e, the state \ket{\varphi}:=R_{y}(\beta)^{\otimes n}\ket{W_{n}}.
\ket{\varphi} lies in the symmetric subspace, and we can express it in the Dicke basis:
\displaystyle\ket{\varphi}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\alpha_{k}\ket{D_{k}^{n}},
(161)
Then,
\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\varphi)
\displaystyle=2\cdot\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^{-1}\cdot\left\lvert\alpha_{k}\right\rvert^{2}\cdot\left\lvert\alpha_{n-k}\right\rvert^{2}
(162)
Identify the symmetric subspace with the spin-j=n/2 irreducible representation of SU(2), under which
\ket{D_{k}^{n}} corresponds to the angular momentum eigenstate \ket{j=n/2,\,m=k-n/2}. Thus,
\displaystyle\alpha_{k}
\displaystyle=\bra{D_{k}^{n}}R_{y}(\beta)^{\otimes n}\ket{D_{1}^{n}}
(163)
\displaystyle=d^{\,n/2}_{\,k-n/2,\;1-n/2}(\beta),
(164)
where d^{j}_{m^{\prime},m}(\beta) denotes the Wigner small-d matrix. We require the entry for m^{\prime}=k-n/2 and m=1-n/2. These matrix elements are well known and admit explicit closed-form expression. For e.g., see section (4.3.4) of [31] which provides the entry we need in terms of Jacobi polynomials. From this, one obtains,
\displaystyle\left\lvert\alpha_{k}\right\rvert\leq{\mathsf{poly}}(n)\cdot\sqrt{\binom{n}{k}}\cdot\cos^{n-k-1}\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\right)\sin^{k-1}\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\right)
(165)
Then, since \sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta is at most 1/4, each term of the summation in Eq. 162 can be bounded by,
\displaystyle\binom{n}{k}^{-1}|\alpha_{k}|^{2}|\alpha_{n-k}|^{2}
\displaystyle\leq{\mathsf{poly}}(n)\left(\sin(\beta/2)\cdot\cos(\beta/2)\right)^{2n-4}
(166)
\displaystyle\leq{\mathsf{poly}}(n)(1/2)^{2n-4}
(167)
\displaystyle=\mathrm{negl}(n)
(168)
Therefore,
\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\psi)=\mathcal{F}_{{}_{n}}(\varphi)=\mathrm{negl}(n)
(169)
∎

should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
all.
